utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to welcome all the parties present in this courtroom. I should like to greet the representatives of the OTP, all Defence counsel, as well as all the staff that is giving us a helping hand in this hearing. I recently sent you an agenda which I'm about to amend slightly because I would like to address a few additional items. Before addressing the agenda, per se, I would like to mention the fact that the interpreting department has let me know that, due to a number of technical difficulties, you have been asked to speak close to the microphone so that we can hear you well and interpret you well. In addition, we have been asked to avoid making too much noise when using glasses or pens or any other objects. I hope that the technical equipment will meet our requirements. Now, as far as technical difficulties are concerned, between now and the commencement of trial, I shall rule on this in writing because I would like to take a decision on the recording of these proceedings and the fact that these proceedings are being filmed. The camera should only focus on the person who is speaking. And when I am speaking, the camera is focussed on me. When the OTP is speaking, the camera is focussed on the OTP. When Defence counsel is speaking, the camera should be focussed on the Defence counsel who is standing. And when it is a witness, the camera should focus on the witness and the witness only. The camera should only focus on the speaker to avoid any different interpretation of the proceedings. So this shall be specified in writing at a later stage. Before addressing the agenda for today, I will take two -- or make two oral decisions. A, given the Statute and Article 67 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, on a motion dated on the 27th of April, 2005, the Prosecution had filed a motion with a view to asking the Defence to notify them of the defence of alibi. According to Rule 60(A)(i) of the Rules, it is mentioned that within a time limit set by the Trial Chamber or a Pre-Trial Judge, the Defence notifies the Chamber of its intent to present a defence of alibi or special defence. This rule comes under the heading of Additional Disclosure, specifies that it is for the Trial Chamber or the Pre-Trial Judge -- the Defence is to inform the Pre-Trial Judge or the Chamber of any special defence. In that case, the Prosecution motion does not meet the requirements of Rule 67. This motion is thus dismissed. In addition, the Trial Chamber feels that it is not appropriate to ask the Defence whether they intend offering a defence of alibi or special defence, given that at any point in time Defence counsel may file a request. So in any event, there is no need for the Defence to notify at this stage whether they intend to present a defence of alibi or special defence. Defence counsel will have enough time, and when it feels it is timely to do so, will have enough time to seize the Chamber of this request. Second oral decision: Given the Statute and the Rules of Procedure and Evidence and 65 ter and Rule 64 -- 54, given that the accused have been granted provisional release by Trial Chamber I. Given that since a provisional release they have not appeared before the Pre-Trial Judge with the exception of Praljak, the accused Praljak. Given that they have been granted provisional release, the Pre-Trial Judge has not been able to ask them whether their state of health was good, given that two recent events have occurred, i.e., the death of an accused and a convicted person, means that the Judges have to pay a very special attention to the state of health of the accused. Otherwise, a trial could come to a halt because of the health conditions of one or other of the accused. Under those conditions, we shall ask the Registry to provide the Chamber with a medical certificate for each of the accused. This should be presented confidentially. This medical certificate should state whether the accused suffers from any mental or physical illness. The Trial Chamber considers that this -- these six medical certificates should be submitted to the Chamber confidentially by the 6th of May, 2006, at the latest. This oral decision is taken notwithstanding the fact that Defence counsel are able to seize the Chamber on the matter if they so wish. This is something I mentioned at the last Status Conference, if they wish to draw the attention of the Chamber to one or other medical condition of the accused. I shall now address the agenda, per se. I would like to -- something which you certainly know about by virtue of a decision rendered by the President of this Tribunal, the Bench has been appointed. I shall preside over this case and I will be assisted by Arpad Prandler. I shall spell his name out for the transcript, P-r-a-n-d-l-e-r. And Judge Stefan Trechsel. I shall also spell out his name: T-r-e-c-h-s-e-l. As of the 25th or 26th of April onwards, we will also have a Reserve Judge who will be sitting and appointed by the Secretary-General of the United Nations. You will be advised of the appointment of the Reserve Judge very shortly. As you know, according to Rule 15 ter of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, a Reserve Judge will attend the entire hearing but will not take part in the deliberations and will not vote on a finding of guilt. This Reserve Judge will only step in if one of the three Judges is unable to attend, either because one of the Judges falls ill or dies or for any other reason. I would also like to state that the President of this Tribunal can also designate a Reserve Judge or Substitute Judge, but this requires the approval of the accused when the said Substitute Judge needs to replace one of the Judges of the Bench. In the event that one of the three Judges that is part of the Bench might have to step down, the Reserve Judge would then replace him or her. As far as the schedule is concerned, I have been in contact with the Registry a number of times last week in order to be able to advise you today the schedule of this case up until the month of July. We have decided jointly with the Registry, as well as all the people concerned in CLSS department, we have decided to hold the case and sit in this courtroom until the month of July. We shall sit in Courtroom number III --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- on Mondays from quarter past 2.00 until 7.00; on Tuesdays we shall start at 9.00 sharp and sit until 4.00 p.m. In this time slot we will have a first session from 9.00 until 10.30, then have a 20-minute break. We shall then resume at 10.50 until 12.20. We will then have a 20- to 30-minute break to enable the accused to have a bite of food. After this 20- to 30-minute break -- it will probably tend to be a 30-minute rather than a 20-minute break -- the Judges will have a glass of water -- the hearing will resume again at half past 2.00. We will then resume at 12.40 until ten minutes past 2.00 and then resume again at half past 2.00 until 4.00. On Wednesdays the timetable will be the same and we will finish at 4.00 p.m. on Wenesdays. We shall resume again on Thursday at 9.00 and sit until a quarter past 2.00 p.m. With this timetable we will be able to do away with a hearing of -- that is usually -- that we usually have on the Friday morning. Therefore, the Defence counsel will have time to talk to the -- their clients on Fridays and Monday morning to address, of course, all issues pertaining to their Defence. The Prosecution will have time to prepare its examination-in-chief, which will start on Monday morning. And Judges will be able to meet and deliberate. Therefore, the schedule has been set until -- between now and the month of July. Depending on availability of courtrooms, there will be five trials ongoing till the month of July, but there might be a sixth trial as of the month of August onwards, which means that this Courtroom number III will have to be shared between -- we will have to share our time with another Chamber. We have a few months' work ahead, which means that the OTP can plan or schedule its witnesses. This is something I mentioned last time, but I will have to address this issue with the two other Judges. We should, normally speaking, resume the hearing on the 14th of August or the 21st of August, but we will keep you informed in due course. As far as the commencement of trial is concerned and the week in which the trial will start, as you know, the OTP will start on the Wednesday, the 26th of April, will present its case. Normally speaking, Mr. Praljak will make his preliminary opening statement the next day. This means that the Prosecution will present its case on the Wednesday, and Mr. Praljak will have the same amount of time to make his opening statement. I don't know what the Prosecution intends to do; I don't know whether the Prosecution needs three hours or four hours. Perhaps at a later stage today the OTP could let us know. So much for the schedule. On our agenda for today I would also like to address the length of time required by the Prosecution to present its case. As I mentioned last time, we have a problem insofar as the Security Council Resolution states that the Tribunal must complete its Trial Chamber proceedings in -- by 2008. I issued an order which you -- has been communicated to you, and by virtue of this order I have asked Madam Carla del Ponte to come here and explain her view of the situation. Madam Carla del Ponte let me know that she felt -- she appreciated the fact that she had been invited to attend this hearing, but she was unable to come today because, as the ICJ is celebrating its 60th anniversary today, and the ceremony was this morning. And this afternoon she is meeting the Secretary-General of the United Nations today, so therefore she is not able to attend. Mr. Scott and Mr. Mundis can perhaps confirm that she will attend the pre-trial conference. Whatever the case may be, the Prosecutor of this Tribunal can attend any of the Tribunal's hearings and the Judges always welcome the presence of Madam Carla del Ponte at these hearings. I don't know where the OTP stands, but at -- perhaps Mr. Scott can let us know and perhaps he can tell us what -- how they're going to proceed. As I mentioned last time, if this trial is to be completed within two years, the OTP will only have one year to present its evidence. I have discussed this with my two other colleagues who have just joined me, and the feeling we have and the feeling the Bench has is that there are two possibilities: Either the Judges intervene at the beginning of the trial to impress on the Prosecution the fact that the indictment needs to be narrowed down, or the Prosecution spontaneously tells us how they intend to present their case and how they can cut down on the necessary time. Before giving the floor to both parties, I would like to remind all and everyone of the following: As I have mentioned before, in this indictment there's three important parts. A relates to those crimes that were committed in a number of municipalities; B --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: No B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two counsel have stipulated that the time at which those crimes have been committed go back a long time ago. The question is whether these -- who has committed these crimes, and this pertains to the chain of responsibility, and this is not challenged. I think if this is addressed in practical terms we shall be able to gain time. B, joint criminal enterprise, which to my mind needs to be proven by the Prosecution and its evidence. And C, individual responsibility of each accused pursuant to Article 7(1) 7(3). There again, this needs to be proven by the evidence of the Prosecution. Subject to these three large areas of the indictment, if the Judges come to realise that the trial is not moving forward, they will certainly react and intervene. There is already a precedent in this Tribunal. In the Milosevic case the said accused was charged with three indictments. At one point in time it had been considered to sever the indictments, to focus on one of the indictments. At the time, this did not meet the approval of the OTP and did not meet the approval of the accused either, but this would have been a tentative solution which would have enabled the trial to move ahead faster. According to the Statute, the accused is entitled to not an expedited but a quick trial; in other words, to avoid any unnecessary loss of time. So I shall now turn to Mr. Scott and Mr. Mundis so that they can let me know whether any progress has been made or are they waiting for Madam Carla del Ponte to come with a turn-key solution and which would enable us to complete this trial within the two-year deadline.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: May it please the Court. Your Honour, I'll first confirm what you've said about Madam del Ponte's attendance today. For the reasons you've indicated, she is not available and sends her apologies. She does anticipate attending the hearing on the 24th of April. We are prepared today, Your Honour, to propose and present to the Chamber and to Your Honour a plan for presenting this case as efficiently as possible. And we are prepared -- to assist everyone involved, we have prepared a presentation that hopefully will assist. May I inquire if everyone can see their video monitors at this point? Your Honour, both in the previous hearing and in the hearing today, has made a number of statements about the completion strategy and that the cases -- the trials of the cases must be completed by the end of 2008. I thought it would be helpful to perhaps look at a few of the statements made by both the former President, President Meron, His Honour Judge Meron, and also a few statements by the current President. We appear to have a technical problem and I will wait, Your Honour. Might I inquire, Your Honour, if everyone now is able to follow the monitor? Your Honour, as I was saying, a few points on the issue of the completion strategy. As President Meron stated in a -- in his middle-of-2005 report to the Security Council: "Any estimates are necessarily tentative, since they can only be based on assumptions subject to unpredictable factors. I could indicate, for instance, that if all possible Rule 11 bis motions are granted, if all possible motions for joinder are granted, if no new fugitives arrive, and if no guilty pleas are entered, the Tribunal could complete its current caseload sometime in 2009. But all of these ifs indicate that the estimates are based on assumptions that evolving reality will modify." Further, in the same statement and report, President Meron said: "Knowing what we know now, the most I can indicate is that trials will necessarily have to be conducted in 2009 and will most likely continue until the end of that year," that is 2009. "When the next six-month report is presented, the President should be able to provide an assessment based on more factual predictions." And indeed six months later, in President Pocar's report to the Security Council in December of 2005, President Pocar said: "In May 2005, my predecessor stated that it was definitely no longer feasible to envisage an end of all trial activity at the Tribunal by the end of 2008. This was due to the large number of indictees and fugitives who had arrived at the Tribunal since the last report, as well as the filing and confirmation of seven new or amended indictments by the Prosecution involving 13 accused. He predicted that trials will have to run into 2009." President Pocar also stated: "In conclusion, I can predict that if the remaining fugitives are apprehended soon, if the cases of multiple accused -" such as this one - "run smoothly, and if the remaining Rule 11 bis motions are all referred without any cases being deferred back to the Tribunal, the possibility of trials finishing in 2009 remains possible." That is, the possibility remains possible. It appears, Your Honour, that both the former and current president of the Tribunal have indicated that these trials will last at least until the end of 2009 and by all indications may well go beyond that. Now, in this context -- excuse me. In this context, the issue of mega-trials, such as this one, has been presented to the international community and to the media as a move toward greater efficiency. That the Chambers of the trials at the ICTY can save time, act more efficiently, by trying a multiple accused cases at one time instead of having a series of separate of trials. As President Pocar said just the other day, on the 7th of April in the presentation to the diplomatic community: "There are at present three trials of multiple accused in the pre-trial stage involving a total of 20 accused, consolidating 14 cases. The first trial -" this one - "will commence on the 26th of April, 2006, and the other two trials are scheduled to begin in July 2006." Now, having presented these trials as, if you will, an institutional virtue, that is as a way of moving forward with greater efficiency, it certainly can nonetheless cannot have been reasonably contemplated that these trials would be short and simple. They are, by any measure, large, difficult, and complex cases. Now, in considering the time limits that have been discussed both in the previous hearing and today, I think it's important that we engage in a bit of a reality check. The international community, the media, the public, and the victims may think that a year is something approaching 365 days, involving 52 weeks, five-day weeks, and seven or eight-hour days. That is when people talk about the case "lasting a year." However, the proposed ICTY year, at least as discussed until recently, and I have not calculated these numbers based on what Your Honour has said just a few minutes ago, but has generally been, and in the previous hearing was discussed, along the following lines, and that is a 40-week year, four days a week, and about three hours of actual witness time a day. Therefore, a proposed ICTY year, far different than a calendar year, the actual time for in-court testimony in a year, on these calculations, is 480 hours. Therefore, if it is said that the Prosecution case, including cross-examination at least equal in time to the direct examination, Judges' questions, and procedural matters, must be completed in "one year," this would mean that the Prosecution would get less - I emphasise the word "less" - than 240 hours to conduct its direct examinations. Now, I can refer back to a benchmark and perhaps we can all refer to our own benchmarks from our own national systems, but referring to my national benchmark, the United States Federal Court practice, a week there is five-day week, seven hours of testimony per day. Based on that calculation, this would require in this court the Prosecution's direct examinations to be completed not in anything approaching a "calendar year," but in fact 34 working days. Your Honour, I don't believe that any fair-minded and intellectually honest person could expect a case of this magnitude, of this complexity, to be presented in 34 days. Prosecution estimates that we made in our Rule 65 ter filings filed in January, let me just say that some fairly inaccurate and sensational things have been said about the Prosecution's proposed case. The Prosecution never proposed - never proposed - to call 399 viva voce witnesses. It was always contemplated that a large number of witnesses, at least - and in fact probably much more - but at least 125 would not be viva voce witnesses. Further, the number of exhibits need not be any measure of the time required for trial if the handling and admission of exhibits are dealt with efficiently. Now, in this context, as I've reported to Your Honour before, the Prosecution has consistently made every effort to move this case forward efficiently in the past two years of pre-trial procedure. For example, we filed a motion for adjudicated facts in April of 2005. We have made extensive efforts to narrow the disputed issues by proposing extensive proposed agreed facts. We've filed numerous motions concerning 92 bis witnesses, including the use of transcripts from other ICTY cases, in an effort to gain efficiencies and save time. We've also filed a number of motions for the pre-trial admission of exhibits. The point and the record should be clear: This Prosecution team has made every effort to move this case as efficiently as possible. Before continuing onward, it's perhaps helpful to just be reminded of the basic point that the Prosecutor -- it is the Prosecutor who is responsible for prosecuting her cases. And the Prosecutor shall act independently as a separate organ of the International Tribunal, and as Your Honour knows, the Prosecutor reports to the Security Council. It is the Prosecutor who bears the responsibility for presenting the cases at trial; at least her case, the Prosecution case. Of course, Your Honour, the -- not only is the Defence entitled to a fair trial, but the Prosecution, the international community, and victims are entitled to a fair trial. Quoting the Appeals Chamber in the Aleksovski case: "The application of the concept of a fair trial in favour of both parties is understandable because the Prosecution acts on behalf of and in the interests of the community, including the interests of the victims of the offence charged (in cases before the Tribunal, the Prosecutor acts on behalf of the international community). This principle of equality does not affect the fundamental protections given by the general law or Statute to the accused, and the trial proceeds against the background of these fundamental protections. Seen in this way, it is difficult to see how a trial could ever be considered to be fair where the accused is favoured at the expense of the Prosecution beyond a strict compliance with these fundamental protections." As stated in the Appeals Chamber ruling in the Oric case on the 20th of July, 2005: "At a minimum, 'equality of arms obligates a judicial body to ensure that neither party -'" neither party - "'is put at a disadvantage when presenting its case,' certainly in terms of procedural equity. This is not to say, however, that an accused is necessarily entitled to precisely the same amount of time or the same number of witnesses as the Prosecution. The Prosecution has the burden of telling an entire story, of putting together a coherent narrative, and proving every necessary element of the crimes charged beyond a reasonable doubt. Defence strategy, by contrast, often focuses on poking specifically targeted holes in the Prosecution's case, an endeavour which may require less time and fewer witnesses." Now, Your Honour, with those observations, I think some important observations, in mind, Prosecution has prepared and will now present a ten-point plan for presenting the Prosecution's case as efficiently as possible. First, Your Honour, we return to our fundamental point and we ask the Chamber again to enforce in a genuine and meaningful way the clear requirements of Rule 65 ter (F) and Rule 67(A)(i). As Your Honour knows, Rule 65 ter (F) requires the Defence to set out in writing: "In general terms, the nature of the accused's Defence; (ii) the matters with which the accused takes issue in the Prosecutor's pre-trial brief; and (iii) in the case of each such matter, the reason why the accused takes issue with it." Likewise, Rule 67(A)(i) provides: "The Defence shall notify the Prosecutor of its intent to offer: "(a) the Defence of alibi; "(b) any --" not just lack of mental responsibility -- but "any special defence, including that of diminished or lack of mental responsibility ..." Now, Your Honour has indicated in an oral ruling this morning, which the Prosecution certainly takes on board, that it really makes the point, Your Honour, that the Prosecution is being confronted with the necessity of limiting its case, of narrowing its proof without having any sufficient information about what the real bona fide issues in this case are, without knowing what the defences really are, either under Rule 65 ter (F) or under Rule 67. As I just said, the Prosecution is being asked to limit and narrow its case without requiring any meaningful engagement by the Defence in identifying the bona fide disputed issues for trial, meaning that under the current circumstances, the Prosecution is required, under potentially very strict time limits, to prove every fact and element whether it is reasonably disputed in good faith or not. What more can any Defence team want than for the Prosecution to consume its limited trial time proving matters not reasonably disputed? Point number 2. The Prosecution can be accountable only for its own time. Should the Chamber decide to impose any time limits on the Prosecution, those time limits can surely only apply and only relate to those functions and uses of time which the Prosecution itself can reasonably control. The Prosecution cannot be responsible for the time taken by the Defence or, with all respect, the time taken by the Court. The time taken by the Defence in cross-examination, for example, might be two or three times as long as the Prosecution in direct examination, and that time certainly can't be charged or marked against the Prosecution's time. In reference to the two choices that Your Honour presented a few minutes ago, that is, whether the Judges intervene early and on their own -- on the Judges' own initiative narrow the Prosecution case, to narrow the indictment, or to give the Prosecution what might be considered a set amount of time and allow the Prosecution to use its discretion, its judgement, as is her responsibility under the Statute, it is her responsibility to prosecute, and then we would have to use -- present our case as well -- as best we can under the time constraints given. And I can tell the Chamber and Your Honour that it is certainly the second option that would be our position. Number 3, the third point of our plan calls for the robust application of adjudicated facts. The Prosecution will make further submissions concerning adjudicated facts, including the relation to the existence of an international armed conflict. If the Security Council and the international community want an example of where the ICTY is not working efficiently, they need look no further than the issue of Croatia's involvement in an international armed conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina during the period 1992 to 1994. ICTY Trial Chambers and Appeals Chambers have repeatedly adjudicated and found the existence of an international armed conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina involving Croatia. The Kordic Appeals Chamber alone affirmed the Trial Chamber's finding on the existence of such a conflict, stating: "The Appeals Chamber notes that the Trial Chamber reasonably came to the conclusion that the conflict between the HVO and the ABiH was international, due to Croatia's overall control over the HVO. On the basis of --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: Stop. [Interpretation] Yes, I stop you now. Let the Prosecution finish, and then I will give you the floor if you want to challenge everything, namely, the decision which was rendered in the Kordic/Cerkez case. So, Mr. Karnavas, you may sit down and you will have the floor later.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: "On the basis of extensive litigation and evidence, no fewer than 14 ICTY Judges (in both the Trial and Appeals Chambers) have unanimously found, without a single exception or dissent, the existence of a relevant international armed conflict ... If the ICTY jurisprudence requires the Prosecution to use its limited trial time --" under serious time constraints that this Chamber may impose, if we're required to prove this matter a fourth or fifth time in this Tribunal's history, then with all and the greatest respect, the jurisprudence is wrong. Point number 4, extensive use of Rule 92 bis evidence. As the Prosecution has previously indicated on several occasions, it will attempt to make extensive use of Rule 92 bis evidence and will take the position that little or no cross-examination will often be warranted. If the Chamber allows it - and of course it will be up to the Chamber - if the Chamber allows it, a very substantial part of the Prosecution crime-base evidence will be presented by Rule 92 bis written statements. Point number 5, substantial use of Rule 89(F) evidence. The Prosecution will also attempt to make extensive use of Rule 89(F) in terms of presenting the direct examination of a significant number of Prosecution witnesses by written statement. In connection with the admission of the witness's written evidence, the Prosecution may supplement or give focus to particular evidence by viva voce questions and answers. In some instances, however, the Prosecution may ask very few viva voce questions of such witnesses. The witness will then be available for cross-examination viva voce within reasonable limits. By this is meant the practice that has come into play or been used at the Tribunal, Your Honour, where a witness is called live to the witness stand; the witness is here in The Hague and in the courtroom, and in -- as part of direct examination, a written presentation of the prior statements are given to the witness, the witness affirms those statements as true, affirms that that statement would be his or her testimony, and then some -- a few questions, or maybe even no questions beyond that, would be asked on direct examination and the witness will be provided and made available to the Defence for cross-examination, and of course also for the Judges' questions. Point number 6, exhibits will be handled efficiently. As stated earlier, the number of exhibits need not have any substantial impact on the time needed to try the case, provided that the tendering and admission of such exhibits is handled efficiently. As we have already indicated and as there has been discussion in previous Status Conferences and as the Chamber -- as Your Honour has appeared to, in fact, direct and to approve, the Prosecution will offer the vast majority of its documentary evidence by tendering a particular document collection, whether it's the ECMM documents or whether it's the Spanish Battalion documents or some other collection of documents early in the trial through a single witness, with the understanding that additional foundational or documentary witnesses will not be required. Point number 7, dossiers will be used, or we propose that they will be used, for much crime-base evidence. The Prosecution proposes the use of crime-base dossiers which will compile the evidentiary material for a particular crime base, municipality, or camp. Each dossier will include a written overview of the crime-base evidence from the indictment and the pre-trial brief and will contain the witness statements and documentary and other evidence relevant to the particular crime base. Pursuant to Rule 65 ter (F), the Prosecutor will yet again ask the Court, based on the dossiers, to require the Defence to identify the specific matters in the dossier which are disputed and to state, as the Rule requires, "the reason why the accused takes issue with it." Based on that, the in-court evidence that the Prosecution actually needs to present can focus on the actual bona fide disputed issues. Now, on this point, Your Honour, we have brought with us today five binders as an example for what would be the Gornji Vakuf dossier, to be provided to Your Honour in just one moment. Perhaps the usher could assist. If the Chamber has -- and I will explain it at length orally -- I will explain it and what it will be, that the binder, the first binder would include the table of contents, including the excerpts from the pre-trial brief and the indictment, and also a list then of the proposed viva voce witnesses and a list of the 92 bis witnesses and a list of the relevant exhibits. We would propose in the future, Your Honours, as to the Defence, that we would present these in an electronic format; that is, if you might call it an electronic dossier beyond the table of contents so that the dossier -- the items in the dossier would be placed, for example, on a CD and could then be accessed and reviewed by the Defence as part of a single CD or DVD collection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may interject, Your Honour. I hate to -- I don't wish to interrupt, but this would amount to be - and I say this with all due respect - what I would consider sort of an ex parte conversation between the Prosecution and the Judge. We don't have these binders. We weren't provided with this. We don't have any way of checking. I assume that they're going to, at some point, give it to us. But needless to say, if they're going to be making this dog and pony show, as we would say back in the States, they should at least give the Defence the opportunity -- the ability to look at this evidence in advance or even presently, not just for His Honour. But I do appreciate that the fact that they now want to introduce this new concept called a dossier which does not exist in this particular jurisdiction, but needless to say it is unfair to the Defence for you to have it and for us not to have it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [French on English channel]. [In English] So there are new rules -- in this courtroom you cannot move. So I of course join my dear colleague and hat those are really the arguments. I would like to add just two sentences. If I understand correctly, we are -- The Defence is a party in these proceedings, an equal party as the Prosecutor is. So if we would have been supplied by this material, at least this morning which would be probably very impolite, but a day or so ago so we can participate in this discussion on equal terms, I would appreciate that. I think that this is just one demonstration how actually the Prosecution is contributing to the fast proceedings, by creating problems in the middle of another discussion without notifying the other party what's going on. Perhaps in some circumstances we might have been cooperative, we might have contributed to something -- some elements to speed up proceedings. We can't. No way. This is the first time we are seeing some ideas here on the screen, obviously prepared in writing, still not delivered to us. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You will have the floor in a minute, Mr. Scott, but four minutes ago I received these dossiers, the binders, and I'm going to ask our court deputy to present these binders to the Defence counsel so that they have no objection. There was a fait accompli because they are going to receive these here and now. The Defence counsel will have the opportunity of going through it, just as I've done. You are true professionals, all of you, just as I am, so that you can just sort of see immediately what they are about. Very well, Mr. Scott, you have the floor. Continue, please, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: One moment, Your Honour, we have -- we're trying to get back to where we were, apparently. All right, Your Honour, let me respond. The only -- the only matter this morning was to present to the Chamber and to Defence counsel the concept. Certainly we are not presenting this evidence for substantive consideration at this moment. Of course not. The Chamber -- if we go down this road, so to speak, and if the Chamber wishes to proceed in some such fashion, they will indeed be prepared and provided in advance. Of course. The only point f bringing them and providing them in the courtroom this morning was as one example of the concept of what might be done, and I described orally the contents -- the table of contents of what would be included in the dossiers. I think that's very clear. I'm very happy and I appreciate the fact that Your Honour has immediately made them available to the Defence, and during any breaks or recess this morning, if they would like to review the material, it is certainly available to them. We are not going to get into the substance of the information; it is simply to give an example of the concept or format which would be followed, which I think anyone looking at the first binder can understand within a couple of minutes. Point number 8. Your Honour, because the Chamber is potentially requiring the Prosecution to prove a limited -- what might be considered a minimalist case without enforcing Defence compliance with Rule 65 ter (F) and 67(A)(i), the Prosecution asks and will ask for the Court's firm assurance that it will be allowed to put on a meaningful and potentially substantial rebuttal case, once any bona fide issues are actually identified in the Defence cases, because otherwise we are again operating in the dark, under extreme time constraints, without the opportunity to respond, to identify the bona fide issues for trial. Point number 9. If we're going to proceed in such a fashion, the Prosecution requests the Court's firm assurance that the Appeals Chamber will some day, perhaps, take the same view concerning the "minimal sufficiency" of the Prosecution evidence as the Trial Chamber, by putting possibly significant limits on the Prosecution case, we are required to present a very minimal case. Based on such an assurance, the Prosecution will be better able to shape its case. Now, Your Honour, this is said somewhat tongue in cheek, but the point to be made is a serious one, quite serious one, and that is really the last sentence of this slide, and that is: "There is really little point in a faster trial if it will be reversed on appeal." There seems sometimes, with all respect, to be a bit of disconnect between what the Trial Chambers want to accomplish and what the Appeals Chamber wants to accomplish. The Trial Chambers seem to feel, somewhat greater at times, the need for efficiency and the need to move the cases forward with some dispatch, but I'm afraid, Your Honour, that some years from now when the Appeals Chamber is combing the record strictly and looking over every detail and dotting every I and crossing every T, the Appeals Chamber's agenda, if you will, will be very different from the Trial Chamber's agenda. And as I will just repeat again, there is little point in a faster trial that is then reversed on appeal. Number 10, the Prosecution may, based on all these previous points of its plan, the Prosecution may be able to complete its direct examinations in 450 hours. Now, since we last met, Your Honour, the Prosecution has undertaken a further extensive review of its witness list and time estimates. On the basis of the above terms, the points that I have made so far this morning, and only on such basis, the Prosecution believes that it may be able to complete its examinations in chief in approximately 450 hours. The earlier -- by contrast, the earlier estimate for direct examinations of the Prosecution viva voce witnesses was 804 hours. That was the number in our 65 ter filing in January, so I think the Chamber will see that we have made a substantial reduction in our time estimate based upon the points of our plan; not 804 hours but 450 hours. Further, the Prosecution commits, Your Honour, to continuously evaluate its evidence, seeking to reduce, to the extent reasonably possible, the time required to prove its case as the trial unfolds. The realities of a trial, Your Honour, as you know -- as you well know, is that things happen as the trial unfolds from day-to-day and week to week. Certain things become undisputed and it becomes clear that certain things in fact, once the trial begins, are not disputed, and therefore the Prosecution can then, to some extent, begin to shape its evidence based upon what the real issues in the trial appear to be, and we will certainly undertake to do that. Now, one calendar year. If the total combined Defence cross-examinations is also 450 hours, that would be a one -- so-called one-to-one ratio, that would be 450 hours for the Prosecution case and 450 hours for the Defence case or cross-examined -- excuse me, cross-examinations. And then if a hundred hours is allowed for Judges' questions, procedural matters, et cetera, that brings us to a total of 1.000 hours: 450 plus 450 plus 100. On the basis of the above terms, the Prosecution case, including cross-examination, et cetera, might be completed in one calendar year if the Chamber were to sit 47 weeks, five days a week, with four and a half hours of actual testimony per day. On that basis we would have some chance, perhaps, of completing the Prosecution case in one calendar year. The Defence case. Your Honour, we feel the need to make the fundamental point that of course if the Prosecution, which has the burden of proof, is limited to "one year," including cross-examination, Judges' questions, and procedural matters, then the combined Defence cases will also be limited to a similar "one year" and subject to all of the same constraints and requirements as the Prosecution, including the scheduling and linking of all Defence witnesses and exhibits to the issues raised in the indictment. In closing, Your Honour, I have a couple more slides to go. We repeat again: The Prosecution is also entitled to a fair trial. We are entitled to a fair opportunity to present our case. Again, quoting Aleksovski: "It is difficult to see how a trial could ever be considered to be fair where the accused is favoured at the expense of the Prosecution beyond a strict compliance with certain fundamental protections." Again, the Prosecution plan, the ten-point plan that we have given you this morning, Your Honour, is contingent on various assumptions and on all of the points being accepted, working in conjunction with one another. In conclusion, the Prosecution plan is based on ifs and assumptions subject to unpredictable factors and we would quote again President Meron's statements in 2005: "Any estimates, including the estimates the Prosecution makes today, are necessarily tentative since they can only be based on assumptions subject to unpredictable factors. " Going to the end of that quote: "But all of those ifs indicate that these estimates are based on assumptions that evolving reality will modify." Finally, Your Honour, the Prosecution commits to Your Honour, to the Chamber to make its best effort. The Prosecution agrees with former President Meron that operating in the ICTY environment is, indeed, a highly unpredictable one, from the changing and unpredictable jurisprudence to the variations and inconsistencies in courtroom rules and practices to the unavailability of witnesses. All of which may make the proposed plan difficult to achieve. Nonetheless, the Prosecution will make its best efforts, and to quote or paraphrase President Pocar, the possibility of presenting the Prosecution case in one calendar year remains possible. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Scott. Before I give the floor to the Defence, let me make some remarks. First of all, I greatly appreciated this presentation of a ten-point plan. The Defence will have the opportunity of expressing their views, and I note that the indictment -- the Prosecution did its level best to move ahead. You had indeed filed motions for facts adjudicated in other trials. You also filed 92 bis motions. You did take measures so that the Trial Chambers -- Trial Chamber can issue decisions for better efficiency, but apart from the efficiency issue, the Trial Chambers issued orders that took into account the position taken by the Defence. The Defence challenges everything, and it is entitled to this under common law. The Defence has a right to cross-examine witnesses. This is how the Trial Chamber had to leave it to the actual Bench decisions on 92 bis motions, 89(F) motions, et cetera. So if your motions were dismissed, they were dismissed on a temporary basis. It will be possible for the actual Trial Chamber to rule again. And this is why I had asked you to give us this chart cross-checking or cross-linking the witnesses, the points of the indictment, and such-like, so that we have an overall view of the issue. And by the 14th of April you were supposed to give us this chart with the links for all the witnesses who are scheduled to testify until July. Once the Judges have your document, they will have a much better idea of the situation. I also wanted to tell you that President Meron and President Pocar had -- had expressed some reservations before the Security Council because, indeed, there are unpredictable factors in a legal process, in a judicial process. This is inevitable. It can be of a very diverse nature, unexpected things can happen. And as you said so for the mega-trials, you know that another two mega-trials are due to commence in July. Ours will start in April, but here again this trial schedule to start in July are not -- are only tentative. Because for one of them, the Mladic indictment could be joined to the Srebrenica trial. So there again it is still a hypothesis and I can say so all the more easily since I am a Trial Chamber II Judge also seized of the Srebrenica case, so I am in a very good position to give you my view on this. Of course if Mr. Mladic were to be arrested, there would be a stage of the proceedings for joining his case with the Srebrenica case, which he can challenge, and he is then free to file any preliminary motions, making it possible to start the actual trial in July. This is the sort of unexpected and unpredictable thing that can happen, and that has to be taken into account. You rightly mentioned something else -- this doesn't call for any special remarks by me, but you mentioned that the Prosecution under the Statute has the duty to prosecute. And when you have the duty to prosecute, you also are fully entitled to prove your case. You also have the full power of deciding what your strategy is going to be. However, this has to be kept within the mandate of our Tribunal. As regards your plan, I am really thankful for giving it to me and for illustrating it as well with the Gornji Vakuf binders. Shortly the Defence will give their position. I personally would like to go quickly through the ten points. In the first point you mention the 65 ter (F) Rule issue and also the 67(A)(i) issue. Under 65 ter (F), the Defence met my time requirements to reply to the Prosecution pre-trial brief. And on the basis of all the Defence pre-trial briefs, there is an overall dispute as to the responsibility. This being so and in doing so, the Defence met the requirements set out by 65 ter (F). It disputes everything, so the Defence counsel do not have to give details as to the dispute. Of course, the Defence could be instructed to do more. When the trial starts, the Judges will see whether it is appropriate to do so, but inasmuch -- and first of all I'd like to remind you that the accused have pleaded not guilty so there is a presumption of innocence and they are perfectly entitled to challenge every allegation without doing anything more, because when they cross-examine or when they present their own case, they can affirm and try to prove their case. Second point, as to time constraints, there is no need for many remarks. This is one thing that I wanted to talk about, to find out how to spread the time or -- between the examination-in-chief and cross-examination. We'll come back to this point later on. Third point of your presentation, this is a topic that caused two lawyers to jump to their feet. It is the issue of the international armed conflict. You said that on numerous occasions this Tribunal at trial level and appeals level - so this is case law - it had been decided that Croatia took part in an international armed conflict. And you said that you were amazed that this was still being disputed since it had been a decision of many Trial Chambers which had been confirmed on appeal. The Defence will have the floor shortly. As to the use of 92 bis, I said that earlier on. To be clear, or to see things clearly, the Trial Chamber will need this famous chart that I requested of you because, indeed, if it were to turn out that 92 bis witnesses failed to bring any additional value to what viva voce witnesses have said, what would be the point of a written statement that would add nothing to the Prosecution case? But to be able to assess this, we would need to have an overview of the case, which was -- which we would have really soon if we get this document by the 14th of April and as soon as we have our first witnesses. Point 5, you mentioned the 89(F) Rule. Indeed, under this Rule you can do away with some of the problems we are faced with. Of course, this Rule can be used by the Prosecution but it can also be used by the Defence when the Defence will present its case. Indeed, under this plan by the Prosecution -- well, you could also think that this is a plan that could be adopted by the Defence. I mean, Judges treat everybody on an equal footing. Why do we have this Rule 89(F) in the Rules? Because it's useful. Indeed, a Chamber may receive the evidence of a witness orally or in writing where the interests of justice allow. So you have two avenues possible. You offered in this respect a modus operandi that could be used, if the Defence were agree to it; namely, that a witness comes to the witness stand, that the Prosecutor has no actual examination-in-chief and offers the witness for cross-examination. But then the written statement is evidence, as such. Your point 6, how to process evidence and exhibits efficiently, I meant to do -- meant to speak about it. I'm sure that we're going to arrive at a solution very soon. The revolutionary part of your plan is the dossier part with the example of Gornji Vakuf. Indeed, we are used to this in civil law, as Judges of civil law, much less so for common-law Judges, but it can be useful and I am going to listen with great attention and interest to the Defence counsel. I had a quick glance at this Gornji Vakuf dossier. The Prosecution, based on the chart I requested of them, could have put into that chart the pieces that we find in this dossier. That's one first observation. I'll add that if, indeed, you have a dossier for the crime-base evidence, which might be useful, I also believe that if the Chamber were to go down that road, you could also have a dossier under 7(1) and 7(3) of the Statute for each of the accused so that we see things clearly, so that we know exactly what the charges are against the accused. It's important, you know, and I would be greatly interested in knowing the view of the Defence because the Defence teams could also have their own dossiers to counter what is charged under 7(1) and 7(3) based on this evidence. As to point 8, the rebuttal case, of course. No problem in this respect. Under the Rules the Prosecution is entitled to its rebuttal case. Why should we deprive it of this right? You also mentioned the Appeals Chamber. Indeed, if we have a faster procedure, how would the Appeals Chamber stand? All the Judges in this Tribunal are aware of the need to change our methodology, and this is the very spirit which led to the creation of the Bonomy Committee, and later and in the next few days there will be, as a result of this work, a meeting of the Judges in order to implement the conclusions, the Bonomy conclusions, and it may even go to the amendment of the Rules because common-law Judges understood that it may now be necessary to have a revolutionary -- a cultural revolution in order to achieve better efficiency. The issue of efficiency is not a theoretical one. Only a few days ago the Security Council adopted a resolution that made it possible to extend an Ad Litem Judge mandate because the trial in which the Judge was sitting was not completed, for instance, and the Ad Litem Judges would have sat for a longer time than the time of his or her mandate. So it was necessary to adopt a new Security Council resolution. But during the discussions that took place in the Security Council, the Russian representative mentioned the issue of efficiency in this Tribunal. The Prosecution, the Defence, the Judges, must heed this factor. It cannot be ruled out. Indeed, we do have a certain budget to run this Tribunal, so it is necessary, and you can't just sort of brush away this issue. Of course, at appeals level the Appeals Chamber will have to rule but you know that the Appeals Chamber Bench is made of responsible Judges. Last point, you mentioned 450 hours, with 450 hours for the Defence; in all 1.000 hours. Of course, I can only agree with this proposal, which is an interesting one, and the Defence will let us know later on what it thinks about it. Just one point I'd like to specify, you mentioned the way in which the US Federal Courts operate and you told us that according to you, because you are an American citizen, the federal jurisdictions work five days a week from Monday to Friday. That's all very well. Let me just tell you that in a US Federal Court there is no trial that lasts for a number of years, so you can sit in a courtroom from Monday to Friday for four to five weeks, but if you are to do this over a number of years, this is something which I come to question. It is now 10.30. We shall have our technical break. The Defence counsel can thus have a look at the Gornji Vakuf binder, and then I shall give the floor to both parties when we resume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we are now resuming the hearing. I shall give the floor to the Defence counsel, who can respond to what the Prosecution has just said. I made my own personal remarks already. As there are a number of you on the Defence team, I don't want it to be going in all directions, so I want you to focus on the essential so that it is something which can be used by the Judge. I shall like to give the floor to Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. It's regrettable that we were not given the ten points in advance so we would be more prepared and more succinct in our response. I assume it is a tactic that we will see over and over again in this court in the name of efficiency, a tactic that is usually used in the courts in the United States where the Prosecution likes to, at the very end, try to sabotage the Defence by presenting novel arguments or novel pieces of evidence to the disadvantage of the Defence. Let me begin by dealing with point number 10, the 450 hours that the Prosecution claims can do its direct examination, a thousand hours in total. I think even under the best of circumstances, and as I understand the Prosecution, they would need more or less all of the previous nine issues, nine points, to be agreed upon before that figure can be reached. I think that is rather optimistic at best, under the best of circumstances. I like the way the Prosecution began by pointing out President Meron's and President Pocar's statements to the Security Council. I think in reality, if you walk the halls of this Tribunal, everybody is talking about 2010 for the realistic date for the trials to finish, 2012, 2013 when this place will be shut down eventually, with all the appeals being completed. I think that's realistic. We did not choose to draft the indictment. As Your Honour knows, the Prosecution has both the responsibility and the discretion as to how they're going to charge. They take into -- a number of considerations into -- when they draft the indictment; the events, the victims, the personalities, and so on and so forth. That indictment then is -- goes forward to a Judge who confirms it. So the power lies with the Judge. The discretion being with the Prosecution, the power with the Judge, and then we get to the Defence. What does the Defence have? Nothing. Nothing in this process at all. So I look at this particular indictment and it has every conceivable mode of liability in it. Now I am told I need to be efficient, efficient in the sense of having a very quick trial, in order to meet some timetable that the Security Council has imposed on this Tribunal because in its previous years, both the Prosecution and, perhaps, the Trial Chambers have been less than efficient. And I say "less than efficient" because if you look at the previous cases and see how much time it took for those trials, which were minor in comparison to this mega-trial, and the resources that were available at the time, the time that was allotted to the parties to prepare and also to present their case, and then you look at this particular case, it's as if we need to hurry-up in order to get it over with. And that I find discomforting. Why? Because we're dealing with individuals. And I think that Dr. Prlic, as Mr. Stojic, General Praljak, General Petkovic, Mr. Coric, Mr. Pusic all deserve a fair trial, and efficiency does not mean a quick and speedy trial. Having said that, going to point number 9, I think that while the Prosecution did say that it -- its -- that point was more or less tongue in cheek, in jest, I think it's unrealistic for a Trial Chamber to give any assurances as to what an Appeals Chamber will be doing. I don't think that the Trial Chamber is in a position to be making deals with the Appeals Chamber or with the Prosecution that if it presents -- if it forces the Prosecutor to be efficient, somehow the Appeals Chamber will be lenient and not overturn a conviction or rule in a particular manner. So I think that's an unrealistic point. Moving up to point number 8 -- and I'm moving backwards because I think that makes a little more sense, at least the way I see things. This meaningful rebuttal, and they say "substantial." Well, I come from a tradition, as Mr. Mundis and as Mr. Scott, where rebuttal for the Prosecution tends to be what we call -- what is normally known as a sandbagging approach, where the Prosecution merely presents sufficient evidence at the beginning of the case to meet its burden, you know, in order to overcome any challenges for a -- a judgement for acquittal. The Defence would then go forward, and then they would save their best evidence for the last, because of course they're playing to the audience of a jury. The jurisprudence in this Tribunal is a rather correct one, if I may say so, in that it requires the Prosecution to put on its entire case, not hold back. They need to put on their entire case. They are entitled to rebuttal but only under limited circumstances and rebuttal does not mean the ability and it's not the opportunity for the Prosecution to strengthen their case but rather to rebut something that was put on by the Defence. So I think that we have sufficient jurisprudence and we need not worry about whether rebuttal will be meaningful or substantial. I think if the Trial Chamber follows the jurisprudence of the Tribunal, which I'm sure it will, then there should be no problem. But this should be a warning to the Prosecution that they should not be holding back evidence in order to somehow spring a trap for the Defence. It doesn't serve their purpose, it doesn't serve the purpose of this particular Tribunal in light of its mission. Now, moving to the dossier. A novel idea. I believe in revolution as opposed to evolution in a sense of how can we make the process more efficient, so I'm all for revolutionary tactics and approaches; however, I think we need to study this more carefully. In principle, I don't see a problem with it. However, it all depends on what goes into that dossier in a sense that if the dossier is presented for the purposes of establishing crime base and if what is contained in the dossier is limited to crime base and not anything else, then I think in principle I would not have any objection, provided, however, that perhaps we could consider that the Defence would be allowed to supplement this dossier. Because part of the problem, as Your Honour well knows, in the Romano-Germanique system where a dossier is commonly prepared, first of all, you may have an independent Judge, such as in France, or you may have a Prosecution who is not a party, in a sense, and that dossier is prepared in a meticulous manner, taking care to make sure that it contains both exculpatory and inculpatory information and it's gathered with equal zeal. Here we don't have that. Here the Prosecution is a party. It's a party-driven system. So I think if we're going to go down the road of a dossier for the purposes of establishing even, say, crime base, I think we need to at least take into consideration whether the Defence should be able to supplement that. Perhaps we can come to some sort of an agreement in advance so that certain crime base information can come in without the need for having to call witnesses and what have you. So I do need to study it a little bit more carefully, but if you look at the table of contents you'll see witnesses there that are rather disturbing to me because they tend to go to substantive matters as opposed to crime base, so I'm a little concerned about that. But the Trial Chamber should rest assured that at least this particular Defence is open-minded to this approach. And perhaps I think this dossier approach could be used for other purposes as well. So we are open-minded to that extent. Handling exhibits efficiently. There was the tendering and admission of exhibits. That was what was mentioned as part of point 6. I agree that a lot of exhibits can come in through one particular witness, for instance, because he may be a custodian witness and the exhibits come in. The question then becomes: What do we do with all these exhibits, all these documents? As the Trial Chamber indicated, as His Honour indicated way back, I believe, two or three Status Conferences ago, that everything in a particular document is subject to being reviewed and being considered by the Trial Chamber, which poses a problem for the Defence because if, indeed, everything will be considered, as it should, it means that the Defence will need to challenge or may need to challenge certain aspects in the document. So having a document or an exhibit come in effortlessly or efficiently is one -- only the first step. We don't have a jury, we don't have to worry about technical rules of evidence; I don't have a problem with that. However, the mere admission of the document is not enough, because at the end of the trial the Judges will be asked to give particular weight to these exhibits; some or none or a lot, I don't know. And that will all depend on how much is being challenged in certain documents. So I think we need to be realistic. If we're going to have a bundle of documents coming in because the Prosecution is pushing them in because they believe these documents further their mission in trying to establish each and every element beyond a reasonable doubt, then obviously we -- you have to give the Defence an opportunity, a reasonable opportunity, to challenge documents where they need to be challenged. And of course, as I indicated in a previous Status Conference, I start with one question: Is this particular question that I'm asking or the challenge that I'm making relevant to the case? If it is not relevant, then I need not make that -- go any further. That should equally apply to the Prosecution. Is a document relevant to their case or is it being brought in because it's cumulative or it's being -- it has more prejudicial than probative value? So I think that some efficiency can occur if, perhaps, they curtail the number of documents that come in that would require us to challenge fewer documents, if there is a need to challenge them. There again, I can assure His Honour that this particular Defence will not be challenging documents for the sake of challenging. Every challenge will be meaningful, there will be a purpose, there will be a reason, and we will be willing and able to state that reason. Whether you will agree or not, that's a different issue. At least in our own mind we will have weighed every piece of every before making any particular objection. Moving on to point number 5, written evidence, a novel technique that was used over here before. I believe it was introduced in the Brdjanin case the first time, although I might be mistaken. I think that's a fine idea. I don't have a problem, where the Prosecution thinks that one need only be cross-examined. That's fine. And again, you know, there's jurisprudence, there's a procedure. The same thing goes with 92 bis evidence, so I don't think that there's much of a problem there. I think we're all in agreement that there's a sufficient jurisprudence to -- to allow this Trial Chamber to move forward on those two matters. Moving to point number 3, I did react in a sense that I believed I was hearing another opening statement, or an opening before the actual opening, or just another argument. And it's the same tired retread argument that we've heard over and over again from Mr. Scott regarding the international armed conflict. He tends to count the Judges as if we're counting sheep, how many, you know, Judges have agreed to this. Therefore, if we come to some magic number, all of a sudden we need not go any further in our analysis. And as I have said in the past, over the years we have learned that archives become available, documents that were once not available all of a sudden seem to pop up, witnesses are coming forward, and indictments were drafted in a rather different fashion way back where perhaps challenges were not necessarily made; or if made were not made sufficiently, at least for the purposes of defending my particular client. So had I been in the Blaskic trial or in the Kordic trial or in the Naletilic trial over there, in anticipation that Mr. Prlic would be indicted down the road, I would have been able to participate, ask the questions. But I wasn't there. So I did react, in a sense, with this particular issue because we already have a ruling on that, number one, from this Trial Chamber. Number two, I thought it was inappropriate for the Prosecutor to be making a mini opening statement on this issue. They will have plenty of opportunity to argue once again when they give their opening statement, which of course is not evidence, as we all know. Moving to item number 2, time limits, and His Honour indicated that we would have an opportunity to speak about the spreading of the time. This is the -- I must confess, you know, in over 20 years of practicing law, this is the first time I am in a setting, in a trial setting, where we are looking at mathematical formulas in order to determine how to arrive at the truth, or at least to make sure that an accused is provided a fair trial. Will 450 hours versus 500 hours be sufficient? Should six accused be allocated, you know, 30 minutes a piece because the Prosecution took X amount of minutes to execute its direct examination. I think that's a wrong approach. I've indicated this in the past. Just to give you one example, and I'm just forecasting. Mr. Donia, he's testified in six cases, I believe. He's produced, you know, some documents, you know, which have been characterised as expert reports. I choose not to characterise them as that, but nonetheless he's produced quite a bit of testimony. And of course with six -- in six different cases you can imagine the amount of evidence that I have to go through in order to cross-examine this man. And if you look at some of his testimony or if you look at some of his writings, he starts with the Middle Ages or before that, the 5th century, 6th century, or whatever, in trying to promote his theory and his thesis. Now, what does the 5th century have to do with 1991, 1992, 1993, 1994? I don't know. But if the Prosecution is going to be introducing that sort of evidence, should I not then start with the 5th and the 6th century as well? I don't know. Maybe not. But the point I'm making is I see this gentleman alone, for me, three, four days of cross-examination, and I'm being conservative. Just to make one point that Mr. Scott had made when he was making his calculations, and I think that they were rather accurate in the sense of how many actual minutes we are in court, keeping in mind that when we begin to have witnesses who speak a different language, everything gets slowed down. And then when you make a comparison, for instance, with the Federal Court of the United States, rarely are they -- do they have these sorts of cases where almost all the witnesses speak a different language and everything has to be translated and slowed down. So -- but my point being, with time limits, I don't think it's rational to assume that we can come up to some kind of a formula. I think we all need to be mindful that everything we do has to be relevant. Point number 1, I don't know what to say. I mean, the Prosecution keeps going on -- I did -- yeah. I think that the Trial Chamber has made its rulings -- or the Pre-Trial Chamber has made its rulings, as it has with the adjudicated facts. I think we need to move on beyond that. We didn't choose the particular indictment; they chose to draft it in that way. And if I may take a couple of moments to speak about what I think was a fungus that actually grew out of control in this particular Tribunal over the years. Unfortunately and regrettably, the Trial Chambers have allowed the Prosecution to draft rather very broad and over-generous indictments, perhaps because some of the founding fathers of this Tribunal were under the impression that we're here to get to the historical truth and to have a historical record. You see the former President Cassese making such statements. Perhaps others thought that this was a way to establish the truth and to get as close to the truth as possible. Others said, Well, maybe this is for reconciliation purposes, we need to have these large trials. And so this Tribunal, in my opinion, has lost part of its focus. Rather than being a criminal court with international law being applied where the responsibility is, at the end of the day, to see whether the Prosecution, which has indicted a particular individual for crimes, be it under 7(1) or 7(3), has met its burden of proof. Some Trial Chambers, along with the Prosecution because of their own mission, have wasted a lot of time, a lot of energy, and have lost focus of what this Tribunal is all about. And so in pursuit of reconciliation or making a historical record, time was squandered on the earlier days. So now we are faced - "we" being the accused in this particular case - are faced with this predicament, that we are supposed to hurry up. Two days ago I was in Zagreb, meeting with my client, and I need to say this because I think it's very poignant, and we were talking about his trip back to The Hague. And I stopped and I thought what it would be like if I were in his shoes where on a particular day I would be making that journey to come here, to be in custody throughout the trial, basically, facing these sorts of charges where, on the other side, the party is doing their level best, with lots of resources, to either make sure that he either never gets out of prison - in other words, that he dies in prison - or that he gets out when he is a pensioner. I mention this because this is what this case is about, Your Honour. It's about individuals. And the charges are very grim. The results of the trial will have impact on everyone's lives, and I don't think because of some completion strategy - because we haven't mentioned that word so much today - that we should try to rush through this case. I share Mr. Scott's concerns when he said earlier that the Prosecution is entitled to a fair trial. Why? Because the Prosecution also has to make sure that justice is not only done but seen to be done. The victims in every case deserve to have their day in court. But as we all know, not everyone who's accused is guilty. I mean, that's something that we need to keep our -- to think about and to consider every day that we're in here. Just because the accused are sitting here and just because the Prosecution believes that he or she has the evidence, doesn't mean -- necessarily mean that they will be able to show that that person actually is guilty, and they are entitled to a fair trial. So I share these thoughts with you, Your Honour, because I believe that at the end of the day we have to make sure that first and foremost everybody gets a fair trial, including the Prosecution. And I dare say their 1.000 hour prediction, even under the best of circumstances, is unrealistic. We will try to be as efficient as we possibly can, but I cannot concede a point to the Prosecution at the expense of Dr. Prlic, you know. In closing, you know, the Prosecution said that -- you know, that they should -- that the accused should not benefit at the expense of the Prosecution. I dare say - I dare say - that has never been the case in this particular Tribunal. I don't think you'll find a single Defence lawyer or accused who will say that he benefitted at the expense of the Prosecution. Conversely, I think if you were to take a poll, you would find that we feel the opposite, that usually it's the accused and the Defence lawyers that are on the short end of the stick because we don't have the resources, we don't have the discretion, and we don't have the power. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I shall now give the floor to the second Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to say that I fully agree with the argument presented concerning the Prosecution point. I fully agree with Mr. Karnavas. I don't think that they need to be supplemented at all; however, I need to reiterate that we also fully agree with your justification and your comments concerning Article -- Rule 65 ter and 92 bis and 89(F). I fully agree with what you said. As for the dossier, I need to add that I personally and my client would find it extremely useful if we had received these dossiers earlier. Had we had them earlier, that would have made our preparations for defence much easier. I also support what Mr. Karnavas said about this. In conclusion, let me add something which supports the position that we all feel somewhat uncomfortable and uneasy about the expected length of this trial. On one hand we all feel this pressure, which is quite human, to make sure that this trial does not last too long because all of the accused are in detention. However, on the other hand, this Tribunal has the largest case before it in this instance with the largest number of accused, witnesses, evidence, and so on, and at the same time, we are urged to make this trial as speedy as possible. I don't think that will be possible. I think that point 10 of the OTP presentation, stating that it would be possible only were the first nine points to be implemented, is too optimistic at this point and I don't think it's a reasonable one. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Madam Nozica. Mr. Kovacic will have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'm going to endeavour to be as brief as possible because my colleague Mr. Karnavas and my other colleague Ms. Nozica has raised all the points I wanted to raise. So all that remains for me to do is to put two or three points forward. We mentioned the right to a speedy trial here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There seems to be a mistake in the transcript. Mr. Kovacic, not Jonjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: It will be corrected, no doubt, Your Honour. [Interpretation] Yes, the right to a speedy trial was mentioned here, which is certainly a fundamental right of accused in this trial in conformity with the Statute. However, in actual fact we are faced with a situation here where we have to take care and strike the proper balance between the right to a speedy trial and the right to a fair trial. Unfortunately, for practical reasons, and I believe that we are all very aware of this, those two rights or those two guarantees of the accused are very often in collision with each other, because a speedy trial sometimes can mean to skip over certain details, to summarise and abridge, and in that process we can lose on the other side; that is, a fair trial. Of course, each of the accused and each Defence counsel, when enabling to strike this proper balance, we have to choose between those two rights, that sometime -- that then it is the more important right, that is the right to a fair trial comes to the fore and the right to a speedy trial comes second. I want to say in saying this that, regardless of the fact that this discussion about a speedy, expeditious trial was caused or, rather, determined by the UN Security Council resolution -- or rather, we cannot use the argument that this is in the interests of the accused, because it is not in the interests of the accused. Very rarely is it in their interests and it very often is in the conflict with the demands and right for a fair trial. And I think that if we start to think about a trial with a stopwatch in our hands, as my colleague before me said a moment ago, it is then difficult to speak about a fair trial, a fair and just trial. Because to be under constant pressure of time, either directly towards a witness or in a cross-examination of a witness, to be under the pressure of a stopwatch and time constraints, we won't reach the proper results. The only criteria is the relevancy of the evidence, that is to say the witness and the documents provided as evidence. The second point that I wanted to raise is this: In a way I have gained the impression that through this type of methodology which is being proposed by the Prosecution or, rather, certain measures that would help speed up the procedure, we are falling into a trap more and more, and that is to speak about the Defence as a party in the proceedings and the Prosecution as the other party, of course, in the proceedings. But when we refer to the Defence and speak about the Defence, we're not talking about an individual Defence but a block Defence team, which is becoming a monolithic block at that. For example, in the division of time, the allocation of time; two hours for the Prosecution, two hours for the Defence, in bulk. And this -- these arguments are the arguments of the Prosecution; these other arguments are arguments of the Defence, in bulk again. Now, we have to constantly bear in mind the fact that we are, in fact, speaking in the plural of six accused and not one accused in the singular, and each of these six Defence teams can conduct their trials, their legal proceedings and Defence case as they deem necessary and to the best effect. Even if it's wrong, it might be quite different from another Defence team. It has the right to provide different evidence, different individualisation, and a different approach.
