And each individual accused in this trial, in these proceedings, is an individual accused person. The aim of the Court is to establish individual responsibility of each and every individual. Therefore, regardless of the accused through force of circumstance or with the other five accused, each of them is still an individual accused. And I think that some of the measures that we're discussing are infringing vitally upon this position of an individual accused before this Tribunal. Now, as far as the dossiers are concerned, the dossiers that we saw on the table by way of an example today, I have just had a look at them and therefore have not had time to prepare and will not be discussing them. But I have to remind because my colleague, the Prosecutor, Mr. Scott, mentioned the Kordic/Cerkez trial where there was experimentation with dossiers. I think the dossier was called the Tulica dossier in that trial, and that was the only one provided and the Defence responded and after that it did not. I am not in a position now - I would have to go back to the transcript to confirm this - but I know that the Trial Chamber gave up the use of that mechanism because for some reason it was not shown to be a good mechanism. I cannot tell you exactly why. Had I seen the material yesterday or the day before, I could have found it in the transcript to refer to it. Now, with respect to the will on the part of the Prosecution to rationalise the case, I would like just to add one more thing. It is my observation, in fact. The Prosecution, for example, when it comes to the existence of an international conflict refers to a series of judgements, and the Prosecution at the same time has completely forgotten those same judgements - here I have Blaskic, Kordic in mind, Tuta, Stela, and a few other cases, a few similar cases, he is forgetting that in those same judgements, in all of them, it was established that during 1992 there was no conflict between the Bosnia-Herzegovinian Croats and Muslims, that is to say the essence and crux of this indictment, and in all those cases it was established with certain finesses of difference or in different areas and different events that those conflicts began after certain incidents had taken place in December 1992, incidents which were not qualified as a general conflict between those two groupings and that the conflicts only began in March or April, depending on the events. Therefore, the time-frame of this indictment ranges from September 1991 to the Washington Agreement in 1994, and despite this, despite the fact that in all these other judgements from which the Prosecutor wants to introduce an international conflict, which they consider to be the proper point, does not wish to introduce those facts which, regardless of the manner of Defence and presentation of evidence were established and that the Muslim/Croat conflict did not exist in 1992. Your Honour, we now come to the question of time, once again. If the Prosecution claims and maintains, and it does in the indictment, that the joint criminal enterprise started from September 1991 and ranged and lasted until the Washington Agreements, it is quite clear, Your Honour, that I have not only the right but the duty, the ethical, professional, moral duty to look at this joint criminal enterprise and the events and to defend that enterprise from September 1991, because that is the framework of the indictment, and within that context present to this Court all the rest of that year, 1991, go through the whole of 1992 in order that you should be able to arrive at the critical time in 1993, which apropos we should discuss from day one. Now, I'm not striving for any change in the indictment. That's not what I'm advocating. I agree there with what the Prosecution said, that they had the prerogative and that's their right, but I should just like to warn and caution that this is a very serious contradiction. The Prosecution cannot at the same time put forward arguments saying that the international armed conflict was proved in such and such a case and then ask that it be introduced here despite the essential differences which Mr. Karnavas has pointed out, which I don't want to repeat now, while at the same time in this indictment completely ignoring all the other things that have been established, such as the conflict -- the time period of the conflict, and so on, and all the other details of which there are many. That's all I wanted to say except to repeat that we have once again arrived at the question of disclosure, disclosure in another form on the part of the Prosecution, to play the game with open cards, cards down on the table. Had we been provided this dossier in a reasonable time, we would probably have prepared reasonable arguments and I would have been able to refer to the pertinent transcripts in the Kordic/Cerkez case. Just one very brief matter, Your Honour. The Prosecution brought up one possible measure that could be applied with the witness summaries, which was also applied in the Kordic/Cerkez trial. That is a specific mechanism, once again, which we could discuss, but I think that we ought to be prepared when we start discussing it so we know what we're discussing because it would demand detailed elaboration, and that is why I can say that in principle I am opposed to that at this point in time, although I personally think that this could be the right mechanism to help us in our deliberations and rationalising our time for the trial if we stick to the rules of the game. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Kovacic. Madam Alaburic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in addition to what my colleagues said, which I fully support, I also wish to give a few comments. Part of our discussion today seems to me to focus on the topic how to fit in one litre of water into a half a litre bottle. It is clear that either we need to throw away half of the liquid or change the bottle, but nevertheless we are still persevering and continuing to try to fit in one litre of liquid into a half a litre bottle. I don't think that's possible. I think right at the outset, at this stage, we need to make it fully known that it is impossible to respect all of the rights of the accused which are guaranteed by international conventions on human rights and also by the documents of this Tribunal. It is impossible to complete the trial by the end of 2008. I think that we need to let the Security Council know, the Security Council which makes decisions concerning the efficiency and work of this Tribunal, that the tasks of this Tribunal cannot be completed within the specified deadline and that the deadline needs to be extended so that the trials which have commenced can be completed in accordance with all the international conventions, documents of this Tribunal, as well as the rules of profession. Even though the Security Council will be ruling on the efficiency of this Tribunal, we will still be held responsible by our clients, by our colleagues, and jurisprudence. Another comment I would like to make concerns holding a trial within a reasonable time-frame. Mr. Kovacic mentioned something known as a speedy trial. Such a term does not exist in any of the international conventions nor in legal terminology or significant legal documents. There is no duty to hold a speedy trial. On the other hand, an accused has a right to be tried within a reasonable point of time. They have a right to have a trial without undue delay as well as a right to a fair trial. These are the rights of the accused regulated by international conventions and they need to be safe-guarded. Naturally this -- these concepts do not pertain only to the accused but also to everybody else involved, either directly or indirectly, in criminal proceedings. However, some other mechanisms were found to deal with the efficiency; namely, either through legislation which provides what is a crime and what isn't, and this takes care of the rights of the victims. In addition to that, the Prosecution is normally given discretion to decide who they are going to prosecute and who not. And when we take all of this into account, as well as reasonable time to hold the trial and the rights of the accused, that makes it mandatory for us to uphold all of these rights. My third comment pertains, once again, to the repeated use of the term of good faith in conduct -- in acts of the Defence. Therefore, it is believed that Defence does not act in good faith if, already in this point of trial, it does not make everybody aware of the facts it denies, the reasons for that, and does not present its case or the course of the case. I believe that such demands put to Defence are completely unreasonable and they go contrary to the basic rights guaranteed by this Tribunal to ensure that an accused, if he so wishes, can remain silent. The right to remain silent does not be interpreted as an act of Defence which is not in good faith. As for the adjudicated facts and international armed conflict, which Mr. Kovacic spoke about, I believe that when it comes to the international armed conflict, we can point to two problems. Paragraph 232 of the amended indictment in our case states that the international armed conflict is based on the overall control which the Republic of Croatia had in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and it is also based on the partial occupation which existed in Bosnia and Herzegovina. To this day we have not received any factual explanation from the OTP indicating precisely which part of Bosnia and Herzegovina was occupied. Undoubtedly the topic of occupation is very important for Defence preparation. As for the overall control, I believe that the adjudicated facts from other trials as to the existence of the international conflict cannot be accepted in our case for these reasons: Because international armed conflict in other cases was established -- its existence was established to decide whether certain articles of the Statute could be applied because there is a requirement for international armed conflict in those cases, whereas in our case international armed conflict is an integral part of joint criminal enterprise, and this goes to the culpability of our clients and their responsibility. To add on to something that Mr. Karnavas said, let me add this: Yesterday I gave our reasons concerning the expert report of Mr. Donia. I don't think that this court exists to establish historical facts. I don't think that this court is expected or qualified to establish the historical truth. We are here to determine criminal liability of the accused in relation to certain crimes, and somebody else can deal with history. In that context, as Mr. Kovacic said, I believe it to be extremely important to ensure that each of the six clients, in accordance with Rule 82(A), is given right to defend themselves as though they were the single accused in the case and that any treatment of six accused as one whole leading to a situation where six persons are treated identically as the Prosecution, which is one whole, I believe that this is entirely unacceptable. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in view of the fact that it's 11.40, and that we're coming up to the time for the conclusion of the Status Conference according to our schedule, I'm going to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Don't worry, we can work until quarter to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, but irrespective of that, I'm going to join in what I colleagues have already said because it would be superfluous to repeat what they've already said using different words, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Ibrisimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I don't want to take up the Court's time in repeating the positions already presented by my colleagues. And as Mr. Kovacic said, in this case there is a disbalance, a disequilibrium. We have six accused here and of course we have six Defence teams and six Defence cases. We're probably not going to agree over all aspects and that's quite normal that if we have six accused we don't all agree over all the facts, and we have to bear this in mind in determining the time necessary for our Defence cases to be presented. The other point is regarding the dossiers. I think this is a mini version of your ruling and order to the Prosecution. I have nothing against this kind of dossier, but I think that this is something that the Prosecution has had to do in double form, and your ruling was that the Prosecution should provide material necessary for the Defence and the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I thank all the Defence counsel; they made a very useful contribution. I'm very thankful to them for it. No remarks following their observations, nothing contrary to what they said. I note, however, that the issue of the creation of a dossier might be an interesting one, worthy of consultations between the Prosecution and the Defence so that they can come to a closer ground of understanding. I see there is a precedent in the Kordic case. The Prosecution had prepared dossiers and for a reason unknown to me and unknown to the Defence counsel, it was an idea that was dropped. Of course, if the Prosecution were to choose for the dossiers, these will have to be prepared for each of the municipalities, not just for the municipality of Gornji Vakuf. So I'm very pleased to see that this idea is not denied. You do seem to have doubts as to the allocation of time, as to the thousand hours that would be needed for the trial. You think more time will be necessary, I do take note, but we have to start somewhere in life so this could be a starting point. It would be possible to extend this time if need be. I wanted to talk about an idea that was tackled by the Defence counsel, the idea of the historical truth to be established. As was stated by the Defence counsel, we're not here to make history, it's not up to us to do so. If you have a historical witness, is he really necessary? He may be necessary in order to remind us of specific data that are not likely to be disputed. Let me give you an example in my national history. You know when the Bastille was taken on the 14th of July, 1789. If a historical witness were to come and say that it was taken then and that in a footnote the Tribunal would say it was repeated, this is not a Tribunal making history, it simply makes references to a -- an accepted version of history. Now, if somebody were to say: No, it was not on the 14th but on the 15th of July, well that sort of a position would be noted. But let's be clear about this: A historical witness is not here to deliver a historical truth to the Judges of the Trial Chamber. The Judges can very well make the difference -- or a distinction between the historical truth of something that is not disputed and something that would be tantamount to speculations. Regarding Witness Donia, he testified in various trials, on six occasions. One of the first trials was the Blaskic trial, and straight after the Prosecution case Witness Donia testified - see the transcript in the Blaskic case - the Defence did not know that he was an expert witness because his name had not been noted by the Defence counsel because the name had been spelled wrongly, Dornia, with an R, instead of Donia, and the research officer of the Defence team had not therefore seen that this witness was going to speak to historical matters. Your deadline was the 13th of April with regard to your remarks on this witness. Of course he's going to testify, but this is the reason why I now turn to the Prosecution, as was rightly pointed out by Mr. Karnavas. There's no point in him talking about the Middle Ages. The Prosecution will have to focus their questions on the very substance which is the contents of the indictment. And, more specifically, on historical points that may be of interest to the Judges; namely, the issue of the creation of a Greater Croatia or the Banovina between 1939 and 1941. That's important. So focus on that rather than what happened in 1341, because I mean, intellectually I'm curious enough to read Donia's testimony in the Blaskic case and I compared a statement with the Blaskic judgement. In the Blaskic judgement there are a few footnotes related to this witness. So what's the point of wasting a lot of time if it's really useless? Both parties must understand, then, when a witness comes to the stand, it is to enlighten the Judges. So your questions must be found in a judgement. If you put questions that have no interest, just don't put them. In this way, both parties will be efficient. Because you put your questions for the Judges' sake because they are the ones who have to rule on the relevancy and also on the probative value of the evidence that was adduced. So this is what I wanted to say after the Defence counsels' contributions. I am pleased as to the general setting they addressed. No further comments on this. Only this, Mr. Scott: For the Judges to see clearly - and also this is for the sake of the Defence counsel - you stated that as you saw things, you would need roughly 450 hours for the presentation of your case. It would be useful for the Judges and the Defence to have an idea of how you're going to break down this time witness by witness. How many hours for Donia? Two hours? Three? 40 minutes? I don't know. Witness 115, how much time? 118, how much time? So I am now issuing an oral decision whereby I instruct you to file submissions stating tentatively how much time you will allocate per witness, to have a better idea. And for the Defence to be able to say, No, you forecast four hours, that's not enough. This is a good way to move ahead. So let's leave this subject because we're got other, equally important issues to deal with and I am afraid that we might not have enough time to deal with them all because this is going to be our last Status Conference. And next time we meet, indeed, it will be a pre-trial conference, which is designed to put a foot in the door of the trial. So we've got other things to deal with then, but now we have to move forward. In order to do so, I have to talk about the issue of the Defence counsel. Two major problems have arisen. I'll mention them in open session. No reason to do this in secret. Inasmuch as this issue may have serious, enormous consequences on the way the trial is going to unfold. One of the accused - let's not name it [as interpreted] - the Coric accused, he wants to have another lawyer. He made submissions and yesterday the President of the Tribunal denied the motion. As a Judge, as the Presiding Judge of this Trial Chamber, when the trial opens I'm going to be faced with the following situation: One of the accused does not want to be represented by his lawyer. As a Judge, I cannot take part in a parody of justice. I cannot start a trial if one of the accused rejects his lawyer. This cannot be done. Therefore, we'll have to find a solution. There are many options, but I'll have to deal with this during the pre-trial conference with Mr. Coric. The first possible option is that he would defend himself. Of course, this is bound to raise another problem. Rule -- the practice direction on the assignment of counsel, and it's Article 13, provides for a similar situation: "When an accused files a motion for assignment of counsel and this is denied, he can file a motion with the Trial Chamber, and it is the Trial Chamber that has now jurisdiction, not the Registrar or the President. And within two weeks, a decision has to be made. The Trial Chamber can confirm the decision by the Registrar or decide that the accused can pay for a counsel of choice or decide that counsel must be assigned." So during the pre-trial conference I shall mention this problem with Mr. Coric. I shall ask him what he wants to do, what he has decided to do. Should Mr. Coric insist on having another counsel, and in the case when the trial has started, the counsel he now has will have to start the trial and stay in the trial for a certain period of time. This is what the practice direction says. The best solution would be that the co-counsel who would be appointed would take over later on. That would ensure that there is no problem, but I say this very solemnly: It is out of the question for me to take part in a trial in which the accused or an accused would not be represented by a counsel of choice, a counsel he trusts. If we were in a civil law system, at a stretch, it could be done because the Judge can then step in, put questions directly to the accused. And even if the lawyer does not do that job properly, that can be done. But this is not so in this system, this adversarial system which is ours, because the counsel represents the accused. The counsel is the one who cross-examines the witness by putting their own questions. But it goes beyond this. The counsel also has to prepare the next stage of the proceedings, which is the collection of exculpatory or Defence evidence. So there is a lot of work to be done in full trust, in a spirit of confidence, between the accused and their representative, failing which there is no fair trial. So I'm very clear on this issue. It must be dealt with when Mr. Coric is present, and he will have to tell us exactly what he wants to do. It is, indeed, obvious. If we had only one accused, this is -- this would be much more manageable, but we have six accused, many lawyers. And the situation arising from one accused should not have a negative impact on the fate of the other accused. And if there is a waste of time because of one, this should not have any bad consequences for the other accused. Therefore, the Judges must be really attentive to this. It is true that the practice direction does give powers to the Registrar. He can, in the interests of justice, intervene. And of course the President of the Tribunal has jurisdiction to decide on any challenge of an administrative decision made by the Registrar. But it is in the superior interest of justice for a trial to be in the best possible conditions and for an accused to fully trust his counsel. I've said this repeatedly in the past: The experience of this Tribunal shows that if there is no such confidence, it happened that at the appeals stage an accused who had been found guilty would challenge this verdict by putting the blame on the fact that he had been badly represented by his lawyer. So for an accused to be well represented, the very minimum condition is that he fully trust his lawyers. I just wanted to mention this to you so that we can find a solution during the pre-trial conference. Second problem related to counsel -- yes, did you want to take the floor?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Just one sentence. Your words are the first news that the President has made any kind of decision with respect to the demands of my client; and on the other hand, I did not oppose that request, and I stress that the confidence and trust between counsel and the accused is a vital prerequisite for a proper defence and that that right should be more important than any right or practice of the Tribunal or of any other courts all over the world.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much for your contribution. This, indeed, supports my remarks, my previous remarks. So we'll come back to this later on when Mr. Coric is here, since he's not able to tell us now what he wants. Second issue: We now have a Reserve Judge who can replace a judge, if necessary. In a trial which may take a thousand hours - and this is a conservative figure - if a Judge is taken ill or breaks his or her leg, his fellow Judge must be able to stand in for him. The same should apply to the Defence team. There should always be two Defence counsels. And for the -- we have to date some accused who have two Defence counsels, but if I look at the list, I see here that for the accused Petkovic, Ms. Alaburic is his sole Defence counsel for the accused. So I've looked into the matter and I know that between Ms. Alaburic and the Registry they are trying to work something out. I hope that a solution will be found very shortly so that you will be assisted by co-counsel. As you know, the practice directive pertaining to the appointment of a counsel states very clearly that the counsel must meet a number of prerequisites. Some of the requirements have to do with a professional with the experience of said counsel. The said counsel must have been in that job for at least seven years. The Registry then looks into the requirements to see whether the person is appropriate or not. This is something I wanted to remind you of and I hope that we will find or come up with a solution very quickly so that there are at least two Defence counsels for each accused. When I say "at least two," this is a conservative figure because you have a very tall task ahead of you and this means that it is better to share the workload and sometimes it's even better to be three. So I hope that when this trial will start up on the 26th of April, all the Defence teams will have an appropriate number of lawyers. Ms. Alaburic, if you'd like to say something, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to say that on Monday I addressed the Trial Chamber with an extensive submission to determine that my colleague, Attorney Miljanic, who is on the team with me and has been since April 2004, should be a subject of discussion and decision with respect to two questions concerning conflict of interests and his possibility to be engaged on my team regardless of what position he holds in the team. And the second question was relevant experience. That was the subject. In my opinion, the -- there was a difference of opinion between myself and the Registrar as to relevant experience, so I think that that is another question that the Trial Chamber should rule upon. Mr. Orsat Miljanic, for example, is -- has a different name on the list of teams. He is informed of all the colleagues -- he knows all the colleagues on all the different Defence teams. He has taken an active part on some issues, and he is the sole person that has all the legal knowledge and facts at his disposal so that if anything, God forbid, should happen to me, if I fall off a bicycle or whatever, he can come into this courtroom and replace me and ensure the unimpeded continuance of the trial. I hope the Trial Chamber has received my motion and that it can deal with it, and I expect the Trial Chamber to evaluate all the documentation, all my correspondence with the Registrar, the Prosecution, concerning this matter and that it will give me a positive response and on that on the 25th we'll enter this courtroom with a co-counsel who is fully competent and fully apprised of all the legal aspects of this case and he would be my co-counsel and associate. And if anybody is interested in having a good co-counsel for General Milivoj Petkovic, then it is me as the lead counsel. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was useful. Mr. Scott, just a second, please, because I -- I'll give you the floor later on. I wanted to respond to what Ms. Alaburic said. This was very useful for the following reason: You've just told me that you have seized the Chamber. I have not yet received your submissions, but let me remind you of Article 14 of the Practice Direction. When a counsel is being appointed - this is what is stipulated - a counsel can be appointed when the Registry has been able to check that the name of the person has -- is on the list -- on the 45(B) list of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, that the person has no criminal file, et cetera, and speaks more than one language. So there is an administrative proceeding here that has to be taken into account when the Registry decides on one or another person. If the Registry dismisses it at the administrative stage, one can then turn to the President, if need be. I think all this means a lot of waste of time. It would be much better if the Chamber were to decide, but my predecessors have followed administrative routes, whereas here we are in a -- in a judicial system. Whatever the case may be, the procedure should be as follows: If the Registry does not want to approve the name of your counsel, you should then turn to the President. And it is only then that you file a motion and seize the Chamber. This is the procedure which we adopted in Praljak's case. Let me remind you that Praljak had a counsel which was appointed, but the Registry did not approve the name of -- did not approve this counsel. We went through a number of procedural matters, and then at the end of the day the Trial Chamber ruled on this. The Trial Chamber rules on this once all administrative solutions have not been found. So if you -- the Registry does not agree with your proposal and you refer the letter written by the Registry to the President and the President then rendered a decision, and then you turn to the Chamber again in the last resort.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have a decision by the Chamber -- well, not the Chamber, the Registrar, I'm sorry. I mean the Registrar. The situation is relatively complicated. Mr. Miljanic was supposed to be my co-counsel and he entered his name under the list and he comes under Rule 44, the list Rule 44, but he wasn't accepted on the list for Rule 45. And after that, we as a team thought that he could be a legal assistant, and then we'll seek another counsel who, in view of Mr. Miljanic's position on the Defence team, will be able to be somebody who is not as well-versed with the factual and legal aspects of this case. And Mr. Miljanic continued to cooperate on the team until the end of January 2006, that is to say for almost two years, he has been working on the case for two years, when we were informed by the Registry that there were impediments to his being appointed to any position on the Defence team because of a conflict of interest. The conflict of interest, briefly, was contained in the following: Mr. Miljanic was, among other things, from 1996 to 2000 employed in the Croatian embassy in The Hague. Among other things, he worked on matters linked to this Tribunal. He represented the Republic of Croatia in this courtroom. From the year 2000 to 2002, he was the head of the government department for Cooperation with The Hague Tribunal. After that, he was assistant and later on deputy of the Croatian Minister for European Integration, and in 2004, at my invitation and persuaded by me, he came to our legal offices and we worked side by side in the building. At the end of 2006 [as interpreted], we learned that there was a problem of an alleged conflict of interest. We tried to clarify what this was all about, but we did not arrive at a single concrete matter which would be a basis and which would be grounds for considering conflict of interests. There was no conflict of interest. It was not presented from the aspects of jeopardising the Defence of the accused Petkovic, but what the observation made was as follows: The Republic of Croatia was, according to international acts, duty-bound to cooperate with the international Tribunal, go everybody in the Croatian authorities who in any way whatsoever provided material for The Hague Tribunal or the Prosecution can be considered to be a participant in the research and investigation against an accused, and that is to say somebody who worked on the side of the OTP and for the OTP. So basis on -- based on my memory, I will quote Mr. Scott. He said that it was as if the -- this individual worked for two opposing sides. I consider that a presentation of this kind of the duties conducted by the people in Croatian institutions cooperating with The Hague Tribunal is completely unfounded because the government office is also duty-bound to cooperate with certain Defence and individual Defence teams, as well as to help Defence teams as mediators, to access certain institutions who have the necessary documents. And not to go into too many details what government departments do, because there is a regulation that governs the work of that government department, it is highly transparent, all of us here cooperated with that department as Defence counsel over the past two years, and we know full well that nobody working in that office or department cannot be considered as a participant in some sort of police prosecuting investigation against anybody. So that's what I wanted to say so far by way of explanation. Perhaps Mr. Scott will be able to present certain details about conflict of interests. If he does, we're ready to discuss each of those details and we would be happy to do so in open session, if need be. If we need to clarify this, we can do this quite transparently and openly in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I will give the floor to Mr. Scott, but as far as Rule 45 (B) is concerned, the prerequisites for assignment are as following: This has to meet the requirements of Article 14, have relevant experience in humanitarian law and international law, human rights law, and have seven years' experience as a judge or prosecutor in the field of criminal law. These are the prerequisites. So I don't see where we can come up against a conflict of interest here. But, Mr. Scott, would you like to say something about this, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That's the reason I was on my feet earlier, because I'm not sure -- I wasn't sure how far we were going to go and I wanted to make sure there was no misunderstanding about the situation or about the Prosecution's position. We do oppose Mr. Miljanic's involvement and there are very serious issues concerning his involvement in this matter which I think will be better dealt with in written submissions in which we can detail a number of matters that the Chamber should be informed about, but we do believe there is a definite conflict of interest, that Mr. Miljanic has been involved in certain things in the past that are very contrary to his representation of this client at this time. And if he was involved for some previous period of time, that's unfortunate, but the Prosecution was never informed and never asked for its position. So that's indeed unfortunate, perhaps, but having been advised of Mr. Miljanic's possible role in the case a few weeks ago, we did in fact communicate, at the request of the Registrar, our position, that is our position, and if we get to the point the Chamber wishes to consider the matter, we will make extensive written submissions on that which will detail Mr. Miljanic's problems. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you say that the Prosecution is of the view that there might be a conflict of interest. I don't know the reasons for that, but I shall await your submissions and we shall rule on this matter once we have been provided with the relevant material. I shall now move on to the other points which are -- other items which are on our agenda. In item 2, we had talked about the time allotted to the Defence. This issue was raised already. If I am to sum up the position of Defence counsel, you have all clearly stated that it is very difficult to narrow your time to something specific. This has triggered the following remarks on my part: This is not a new issue in this Tribunal. I would like to refer you to the Kupreskic case and the Kvocka case. This issue was also addressed in those two trials. In the Kupreskic case it had been -- the Bench had specified -- let me remind you that there were a great number of people involved in that case. When the Prosecution had a specific allotted time, the Defence overall had -- was allocated the same amount of time. To be more precise, if the Prosecution has two hours, the Defence then also had two hours, and those two hours were divided between the accused. If there were four accused, you had to divide those two hours by four. So much for the Kupreskic jurisprudence. In the Kvocka case, the same principle had been applied. If a Defence counsel did not wish to use up his or her time, another Defence counsel could benefit from his or her time. As far as this Chamber is concerned, it's a matter of course which I will, however, have to refer to my fellow Judges. But what I had said initially, which I think is a good guideline, it would be appropriate to make a distinction between the facts on the one hand and the individual criminal responsibility of each accused on the other hand. As far as the facts are concerned, you had the dossier Gornji Vakuf in front of you a few minutes ago. Gornji Vakuf is something which pertains to a number of counts. Therefore, can this be dealt with within a particular time-frame by the Prosecution? And then you agree amongst yourself to decide that one or other Defence counsel will cross-examine the witness and the other Defence counsel will intervene if need be. We then have equal time on both sides. You want to avoid Defence lawyers saying the same thing and duplicating what has already been said. So it is a matter of rendering this as efficient as possible. So it would be beneficial for the Defence to respond as following -- I'm just quoting Gornji Vakuf by way of illustration. The lawyer who would be cross-examining would focus all his attention on the cross-examination of the witness. The other Defence counsel could then prepare further cross-examinations in that time. Then you exchange your points of view, but as you have all said, Defence teams cannot be taken as a whole. I understand that. You are Defence counsel of particular accused who have been charged with particular crimes. Therefore, once we are going to talk about looting, destruction, abuses, do the six Defence counsel then have to ask the same or put the same questions to the witness? I think this would be very unrealistic. I think it's for you to agree on this and one counsel should be responsible for the cross-examination. Of course, the other Defence counsel can stand up and say something if they so wish, but I think we have to settle this issue. When we will address JCE and individual criminal responsibility, then of course each Defence counsel has the same amount of time. There is no question of having Mr. Prlic's Defence counsel cross-examine the witness in the name of Mr. Praljak. It's then Mr. Prlic's individual criminal responsibility which is at stake, so that wouldn't work. You have to consider this and understand that we have a time constraint, because as I've mentioned in the order I issued, if I were to calculate all of this, three years for the Prosecution, three years for the Defence, we would still be here in 21 years' time. So I think you have to agree on this amongst yourselves. I know there may be differences between you, but some witnesses will be called to testify -- let's take the case of Mr. Donia. When Mr. Donia is called to testify, do you each need to cross-examine him? Unless, of course, you feel that you need to put a very specific question because it relates to your Defence case, and I think there are economies of scale that could be achieved when Mr. Donia is being cross-examined, for instance. This means that you have to discuss this matter beforehand and work out the way in which you are going to proceed with your cross-examination. You can even prepare a plan, if need be, a work schedule. This might be more interesting if you all go into the battle at different times. So you have to find a solution. We are a few ways away from the beginning of this trial and we still haven't come up with a solution. What we could say is that the Trial Chamber renders a decision and then you just have to abide by that, but I think it would be much better to find a solution on a consensus basis. So as I think it is better to have a consensus, I shall give you all the floor. The Prosecution, do you have an opinion on this matter? Do you have something to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, our position is the one that we've stated, that, for practical reasons, including the fact that the Prosecution has to schedule its witnesses with some specific number in mind, we just can't simply wait, whether it's two hours, two days, three weeks later, and then have the next witness come, we have to make very, very practical decisions on when to schedule the next witness. So until, as Your Honour says -- and since we've been talking about this since November, so something like six months now, without any resolution, the only resolution is that the general rule of thumb be that it be a one-to-one ratio; one hour for the Prosecution and one hour for the Defence combined, unless some very compelling justification or exception can be shown.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Karnavas, it's now 20 past 12.00. We have to have a 20-minute break. In this time, you get together with your colleagues, find a solution, and in 20 minutes' time you'll have the floor. The hearing stands adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Karnavas, you now have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just a couple of observations I wish to make with respect to the timing and cross-examination. First of all, the Prosecution may choose to put on a very limited direct, leaving out areas which the Defence may feel are relevant. Clearly, under those circumstances, the Defence would be entitled to go beyond the scope of the direct examination. I don't think that there is any question about that. As long as the area is relevant, the Defence should be able to go into those areas, so -- and I say this because the Prosecution cannot use that for tactical purposes. Otherwise, the solution would be for the Defence to then call that very same witness back in order to do a direct examination in areas which were relevant, and this of course would be timely, would be costly, would be unnecessary. Second of all, I wish to bring to the Court's attention that there may be times when a particular witness, through cross-examination -- you know, the Defence may wish to introduce certain evidence, whether it be documents or go into areas -- question the witness into certain areas, setting up, for instance, a point that will be made later on. So just to give an example, for instance, the Prosecution does its direct examination through this particular witness I have identified where I might be using -- might be able to use this witness as a vehicle to introduce certain evidence, to tender certain evidence for admission, and also to pose certain questions to this witness that were not raised by the Prosecution. Of course, this is a time-consuming process, and it would go -- it would take more time, perhaps, than the Prosecution may have envisaged, given the limited direct examination. I think we need to keep in mind that the Defence can no more control the Prosecution's direct examination; you know, they're entitled to put on their case. I can't put on any limitations, and I certainly can't force them to go into areas of direct examination which might be relevant and might be exculpatory for the Defence. On the other -- they don't have that obligation and I'm not imposing one on them. On the other hand, the Prosecution cannot prevent me from going into areas which are relevant and may be exculpatory to the Defence. And I think there should be no disagreement between the parties on that issue. So when we look at the time allocated, I totally and fundamentally disagree with the Prosecution that it should be one for one. I don't think it's possible and I don't think it's practical. If we're going to proceed in that fashion, it would be somewhat like if we're playing speed chess. We would each have our clocks, and then we would stand up, we would hit the timer, and off we go, and of course if I were to spend less time on one particular witness, I should somehow be accredited with a certain amount of time that I might be able to use with another witness. And then it becomes a charade, where we're each, with our own stopwatch, are keeping track of how much actual time we use in order to make sure that we have this parity one-on-one. I don't think that's what this Court envisages. One last point -- and I agree with Your Honour when you say we, the Defence, should try to work among ourselves. To some extent that's possible, to another extent it isn't. I think at some point we are going to be taking different routes and we have different interests and of course every one of the accused had a different function during the relevant period of the indictment. So we each have our own respective client to represent. But with respect, to, say, accused Coric, if indeed he is given a new counsel who is going to come basically with a blank slate, even if he is to have the assistance of Mr. Jonjic, who in my opinion knows the facts better than anyone else of the Defence, has probably seen more documents than anyone else and, in my opinion, is an outstanding lawyer and a true professional and I'm proud to be a member of the same, you know, company with Mr. Jonjic. But if we -- if he -- Mr. Coric is to have a new counsel who doesn't know anything about this case, I don't see how we can meet -- we can sit down and agree to allocate time with someone who may not know what is or isn't relevant. So there is that added concern. And I think there's some technical issues that we need to keep in mind, and I go back to what I fundamentally said before: If the area is relevant, nothing should prevent Defence counsel from going into that -- those areas, making -- asking the relevant questions, and then moving on. I know that if I'm not permitted to go into certain areas which are relevant, I can anticipate what I'm going to be doing because I've done this before in cases in the United States where the Judge wanted the process to move along, because I think Judges all over the world are basically the same; they all want the case to proceed as efficiently as possible and they're all worried about their calendars, and that's rightly so. On the other hand, what I would normally do is I would present a list of areas that I thought were relevant in order for me to preserve the rights of my client and to make the appropriate record. Normally, with some discussion, we are always able to find an elegant solution where perhaps the Judge would say: Well, maybe this area is already established, this is not necessarily relevant, but I'll let you have a certain amount, and normally we were able to find some solution. But in any event, that would be my approach and I just say -- I just say this for the record, that perhaps this is something the Trial Chamber should consider, keeping in mind always that we are representing different clients with different interests and we have different theories with respect to many areas of trial. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you. Once again I have to fully support what Mr. Karnavas said. I need to add three important issues. The first one is that the proposal advanced by the Prosecution to have time ratio split one-to-one is generally unacceptable for all the reasons mentioned by Mr. Karnavas. If we analyse the case as a whole, I think there will be situations where Defence will not use its right to cross-examine, or it will use up much less time than the Prosecution used in examination-in-chief. As for any possible agreements among Defence teams, sometimes that will be possible. When it comes to general questions, to witnesses giving evidence about all of the accused together, without going into individual responsibility, yes, in those cases it will be possible to agree and we will inform the Chamber about that. As for the third, I think that it is beyond dispute that all Defence teams will be putting only relevant questions in their cross-examination and that there will be no repetition mentioned by you. I think that ultimately we have proven that to you by our conduct in Status Conferences. Therefore, we do that in all cases where it is possible for us to agree with what was said previously so that we don't use up anybody's time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it seems I don't have much to add. Mr. Karnavas and Ms. Nozica said everything that I agree with. I think that Mr. Karnavas perhaps did not articulate clearly enough the other controlling element, and that is this: The time used up by Defence in cross-examination has to be controlled by two standards; the first one is relevancy and the second one is avoiding repetition. I think that both standards are in the hands of the President of the Trial Chamber and that you will always be able to ask for a clarification as to why a certain question is important or relevant for Defence, and you will either get a satisfactory explanation or not. And then you will be able to discontinue, to order that any further cross-examination be discontinued. When it comes to repetitive questions, then naturally the same applies here. It is possible that, say, the sixth Defence counsel repeats the question put before. Yes, those instances are possible, but they shouldn't be applied as a rule. Another matter that we have to keep in mind is that we have witnesses that belong to various categories and will give evidence about various facts. Based on the lists that we have seen, it seems that the Prosecution intends to call a lot of witnesses to testify about the existence of joint criminal enterprise, the control exercised by Croatia, and so on. Therefore, I think that there -- in those cases there won't be a great need for each Defence counsel to examine -- cross-examine witness in detail because there will be little left for the one who comes last, other than to put repetitive questions. And I think that we might see an unwanted impact here because it could be that the third or the fourth Defence counsel to stand up will have nothing to say because everything will have been covered by then. And then the next category are the witnesses testifying about minor events. If my client has nothing to do with those minor events, then naturally I won't be putting any questions. I might ask something just to clarify some minor details, but other than that I won't have anything. So we have different kinds of witnesses which means that Defence teams will use different approaches. I think the only approach to an efficient control of time is to stick closely to these traditional elements which are relevancy and avoiding repetition. As for the allocation of time, which is a method applied in many courtrooms but, once again, not applied in many other cases - and both positions can be defended - I think that the allocation of time would produce this stopwatch trial and that would result in all the technical difficulties that my colleague mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as for the allocation of time, I have four points to present. I think that the length use -- the length of examination-in-chief is not relevant to determine the time needed in cross-examination because we not only have to deal with the substance of examination-in-chief but also with the substance of documents which are tendered through that particular witness as well as the substance of the statement or evidence given by that witness. So when we take all of that into account, then that is the entire quantity of time needed to examine that witness. That, in turn, would mean that the Defence would need more time for cross-examination than what the Prosecution used for examination-in-chief precisely because of the documentation tendered through the witness. So looking purely at the length of examination-in-chief is not relevant enough to determine how much time will be needed for cross-examination. Now, Rule 82(A). I, as one of the Defence counsel, expect that my client will be allotted an identical period of time because he needs to be -- he needs to have the same rights as all other accused. So we have to take the rights of each individual accused separately because those rights are guaranteed to all of them. Third, since we need to plan our time realistically, naturally we must make sure that we are not repetitive in our questions. We also have to count that some events will not touch upon the status of each of the accused. So I think that when rationalising time and when planning time - and this is something that is important for the Prosecution and their schedule - we can be somewhat flexible so we don't always use up one-to-six ratio but can also use some other proportions. Fourth, even if we were to set a mathematical formula, I think the main criteria that should guide us must always be relevancy and if evidence of some witness is extremely relevant, I think we need to allot extra time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I join my colleagues in what they said before me. I consider that a mathematical division of time, the time allotted to the Prosecution and Defence, is not the right way to go about it because it would be to the detriment of the accused and their right to a fair trial. And the only criteria that can be applied and should be applied in the examination and time for examination is relevancy and non-repetition. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is quite obvious that the Defence and Prosecution have quite opposing positions when it comes to the time needed for examining and cross-examining witnesses. I think, in general terms, that this ratio cannot be one-to-one. The Defence will need far more time for its cross-examination. Of course, this should be reasonable and you're probably going to give us some guidelines about that, how to use time as rationally as possible. Now, as for the other question that was raised, that one Defence counsel should ask questions on behalf of all Defence counsel, that is possible on some occasions but otherwise it would be impossible because each Defence team must have the right to ask questions that they consider important for the Defence of their client. I have said this at other Status Conferences: Sometimes there are things that you cannot incorporate into mathematical calculations. There might be a question that is important for either the Prosecution or the Defence, but judging on the experience I have so far, Your Honour, we found an elegant solution, an elegant way around this so that it was neither the Prosecution nor the Defence that was curtailed of its right of conducting an examination in their best interests. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very briefly, just two minutes. What we see here illustrates exactly what the Prosecution's concern is, and that is this: We will have one set of rules for the Prosecution in which the Prosecution time is strictly limited and our entire case is being limited and what we can do; and then when it gets to the Defence side, there won't be whatever rules, it will be whatever time is reasonable. Well, I would like to have that same flexibility, too. I would like to have as much time as I think is reasonable for putting on the Prosecution case. If the Chamber doesn't give me that, if the Chamber says you're limited to 450 hours, or 300 hours, then I don't have the flexibility to be "reasonable." So I have to say in the strongest possible way, Your Honour, if the process evolves where we have one set of rules for the Prosecution and another set of rules for the Defence, that is entirely unacceptable to the Prosecution. In terms of scheduling, Your Honour, as I've said before, for everyone else in the courtroom at the moment and, in all respect, including the Court, these are very interesting but academic issues. This is a very real issue for the Prosecution because we have responsibility for scheduling and getting the witnesses here. In a few days we're going to have to give you a calendar, that you've asked us to do, the list of witnesses and who's coming when. We have to have a set formula for determining when the next witness comes to The Hague. We are not going to have, Your Honour, three or four or five witnesses sitting here in The Hague, waiting, and not knowing how long cross-examination will be. We cannot bring these people from Bosnia and say: We don't know how long you'll be in The Hague, ma'am. You may be there five days, you may be there three weeks, because we don't know how long cross-examination will be. We are going to give you a calendar. If there is no other rule or no other principle that's agreed upon, when we give you that calendar in a couple of days, just so there is no surprise, and I'm trying to be as transparent as possible, we're going to base it on a ratio of something like two or three to one and we will make and plan our witnesses accordingly. And then, on a given day, if, lo and behold, the Defence doesn't use as much time and there is no witness available because we don't have a witness in The Hague, then we won't have a witness. But we have to have a certain formula. It doesn't just float in the air. We have to make decisions and scheduling based on specific time limits. That's all I can say, Your Honour. We simply cannot float around and then call up tomorrow to Sarajevo and say: Hey, all of a sudden we need a witness tomorrow, who can you get here overnight? You know, Your Honour, it doesn't work that way. So unless there is some other resolution, the schedule we are going to give you some days, a few days from now, is going to be based on a three-to-one ratio, and if it turns out we don't have a witness on a given day, Your Honour, just remember this day, the 12th of April, and I'll say, Your Honour, that's what we planned on and it's unfortunate that we don't have a witness available in The Hague, but that's the only formula that we could use.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, could you be more clear as to this ratio three-to-one, which I find on line 19, page 82.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What I mean by that, Your Honour, is that if, for instance, the Prosecution thinks the direct examination will take two hours, we will assume that total cross-examination will be six hours. So therefore when we fill out the calendar, we will allocate a total of eight hours for that witness, which is more than two trial days. And if that time isn't used and, Your Honour, you say to me: Mr. Scott, call your next witness, and if we haven't brought a witness to The Hague, we just won't have a witness, because we have to have some rule to be governed by.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Well, we're moving ahead step by step. The Prosecution is going to give us a calendar with a ratio of three-to-one. Let's take an example. If for the first witness, a female witness, he has scheduled two hours, in this calendar there will be for the entire testimony eight hours, including six hours for the cross-examination and two for the examination-in-chief. Therefore, this witness will be scheduled for at least two hearing days. Now, let me turn to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. First let me go back to what Mr. Scott said earlier about flexibility, because I don't want there to be any misunderstanding. We on the Defence side are certainly not advocating that the Court should not be flexible with the Prosecution. They should put on their case however they see fit. So I just want to make sure that that's -- we're clearly understood on that. And I certainly don't think there should be a double standard, one for the Prosecution, one for the Defence, whether it benefits either side. I think there should be one standard. I think, and I speak for all of my colleagues, we want to make sure everybody's treated fairly, and from what I see, the Prosecution is getting their fair share at this -- so far. With respect to this formula, I don't have any objections to this formula, although I don't want to be -- what I seem to be hearing is constantly the Defence is being blamed for the Prosecution not being able to do whatever they need to do. If, for instance, the Prosecution were to provide us with a list of 10 or 20 witnesses that they anticipate of having, their first batch of witnesses, okay, he wants to be transparent. What is preventing him from being transparent? I haven't said: Don't give me that list. I welcome the list. Give me the list. And then I will sit down with my colleagues and say, okay, this is how much we anticipate from each of these witnesses and then he can plan ahead. So nothing is preventing the Prosecution from being as transparent as possible. But what are they doing? They are waiting until the very last day, and then they come into court and then Mr. Scott always wants to blame the Defence. I think it's a little unfair. I'm willing to work with the gentleman, as all of my colleagues are. He can give us the list. He wants to do it in blocks, then we'll do it in blocks. I understand the difficulties of trying to get someone over here at the last minute. I also know that you don't want to have witnesses staying here for more than one or two days before testifying. So we all understand that. We're all professionals. If we have a list in advance, okay, and if we do it in subject matter, we would be able to sit down and we could discuss with the Prosecution, and there are going to be times when we just cannot agree. We'll agree to disagree. But I think most of the times we'll be able to come up with some sort of an agreement. Because if we say, as a block, that we believe it's going to take X amount of time, we would have to justify why we came up with this particular figure. So if you ask me Donia, three days, I can tell you why. It's not a mystery. So if Mr. Scott wants to give us that list today, we can start working on it this afternoon. And I assume that he has that list. I don't want to prevent him from being as transparent as possible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will be very brief. There is another detail. The Prosecution is complaining that they won't be able to plan ahead, and perhaps for that reason sometimes they will lack a witness or two so there will be some leave time for everybody, or that they will sometimes be forced to keep a witness for too many days in The Hague. That is simply not correct. There is a huge experience in handling the witnesses and planning of their testimony. We are not here -- we are now in, what, 10, 12 years of functioning of this court. The Prosecution is the same team. They have the knowledge. In addition to that, there is a unit which cares about witnesses and victims, which is, by the way, the best department in this court. There is absolutely a perfect experience, perfect management, and perfect knowledge. My dear colleague Mr. Ken Scott was -- we were in the same courtroom in Kordic. I don't remember there -- perhaps it was once, one morning, when witness was not planned for this morning and we lost, I don't know, maybe half a day of the trial. And there we didn't have the time as controlled for the cross. Despite all of that, the planning was good. And I would say that there is also an instrument. After a while, after three months or four months of the trial, then we could make statistics and then you will see that all what is the Prosecutor now promising about three hours for a witness, Your Honour, with all due respect, we will not see such a witness, because in earlier trials the average for the Prosecution was more than a day. About -- one day point two or one day point four for one witness, and it cannot be credited only to the Defence. So planning purposes with the Prosecution is now representing as a major concern is not a concern. Realistically, it is not. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, I have a comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one remark. I simply consider that we must not pass over the opinion that the accused -- that the accused would be -- or rather, would not receive the necessary provisions and that the Defence would be overprivileged. I want to say that I will fight for the rights of the Prosecution equally when they conduct the cross-examination or, rather, if I and my Defence team should be given, say, 200 hours for the examination-in-chief, I shall consider that the Prosecution has at least that much time for the cross-examination. So in the total number of cross-examination hours, the Prosecution will have six times more or, rather, equal to the Defence. So it is equal arms for both sides and equality of arms on both sides. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I feel that this is very simple and that there's just one right solution here, which was stated by Mr. Karnavas, but I want to simplify it even further. Let the Prosecution give us a list of witnesses which they are going to examine during month of May, for example, a list of exhibits which they are going to introduce by those witnesses, and we shall inform them within a time limit which you set, inform you how long we need for the cross-examination once we have reached an agreement. So that's a simple process and we can continue that practice in future and I don't think there will be any problem on that score. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You stole my words, as it were. I was about to say exactly the same. In order to see clearly, it is necessary for everybody to have the chart I asked you to draw up. Secondly, the Prosecution must very shortly give to the Defence and the Trial Chamber the list of the Prosecution witnesses, of course, together with the exhibits to be introduced through the witnesses and the estimated duration of each testimony. The Prosecution can take but only tentatively this ratio three-to-one, and in this way we can move forward. My conclusion is this: Following the contributions by the Defence counsel, I believe that they do all want to be efficient. They realise that we should waste no time. I'm firmly convinced that all of the Defence lawyers will look into your list with great attention, will meet with you, because that's what they suggested, and you will, surely, arrive at some kind of agreement and then you'll let us know. Should there be further points of disagreement, we shall rule on them. Most of the Defence counsel present here have prior experience in this Tribunal. They are familiar with this type of problem. There's no reason to believe that the problem that may arise is insurmountable. No, it can be dealt with. At the very least, to start with, is that the Defence should have the tentative planning for the Prosecution witnesses. Based on that, the Defence counsel will tell the Prosecution how much time they need for the cross-examination, and we might come to an agreement within this ratio of three-to-one. Maybe it will be one-two or one-one, who knows. And if ever there is a real problem, we shall rule. My previous experience tells me that we always manage to find a solution. We must start the trial, and then, depending on problems, we shall adjust the proceedings. You are quite right, Mr. Scott, together with the Victims and Witnesses Section you must sort of arrange your planning for the witnesses to come and then pass it on to the Defence. They will tell you whether they need the same amount of time as you do or twice that time, and then you will tell me if there are problems. We're going to meet again anyway for the pre-trial conference and we can tackle this again, but until then, do give this table. You wanted to take the floor, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just very quickly, because I think the last item on your agenda is the schedule or the charts, perhaps, which we have been preparing and, indeed, I agree that when those are provided, and we will provide a list of all the witnesses, you know, tentatively, because as we indicated before, there could be a chance that someone in the middle of June can't come, but we will provide a schedule in the next couple of days of the witnesses through the July break. There's no mystery about that. It's been on the schedule for some time. I would note, however, as mentioned during the last Status Conference, we gave the Defence more than a week ago the list of our first six witnesses. So that is not a secret. And Mr. Karnavas has already told us that for Mr. Donia, even though the direct examination may only take a couple of hours, that he's going to take two, three, or four days. So that's already exceeding a three-to-one ratio. We'll just agree, Your Honour, we'll see how it does. We'll provide the schedule and we'll ask the Defence to then come back to us in a very short time with their indicated cross-examination so that we can then plan accordingly, but we have to have that more than just a day or two ahead of the witness. They have to come back to us quite quickly, then, based on our schedule, with the stated times for cross-examination, and we will try to go forward on that basis. I would like to say, Your Honour, when we said for planning purposes that we would agree to something like two-to-one because we have to use something and we don't want to underestimate, let us be very clear, that was no indication that accept that as a general principle. We do not agree that all cross-examination should be three-to-one. If there is repetitive questions, and duplicates and cumulative questions, we will be objecting to that. So I don't want to be misunderstood that we were giving approval to a certain ratio. We were simply saying for planning purposes only we had to have some number to use. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Also no comments as regards what you've just said. However, there's something which caused some surprise. You said Mr. Karnavas needed -- would need four days to cross-examine Mr. Donia. I must say this comes as a surprise to me. I'm somewhat taken aback. Mr. Donia might be an interesting witness, but on reading his report and how this relates to the indictment, I would say that one day is quite enough. The Defence will see what is fit, but as far as Mr. Donia is concerned, I don't think we should repeat what was done in the Blaskic case where Mr. Donia was heard for a number of days and the outcome was not very relevant. As far as the Judges are concerned, this was of no particular interest. So I should like to move on to another topic now because I have very little time left. I would like to talk about presentation of evidence in the presence of the witness. As you know, we have the e-court system, but I would like to ask the Prosecution this question: When it will examine the witness and present the documents to the witness, I would like the Prosecution, prior to that, to prepare a little file for me, a file which will contain all the documents that will be presented. I can only encourage you to put this or give this to me in the presence of the witness. Once the documents have been presented at the end of the hearing, you can stand up and you can ask that these documents, P620 to P640, 3.020, so 1500 and so on and so forth, be admitted into evidence. This is how things should unfold. That said, it's not because an exhibit has been admitted into evidence that it is automatically relevant or that it has any probative value and that this will catch the attention of the Bench. As I have said, from the outset you need to adopt -- you need to present your exhibits, when the Defence during its cross-examination wishes to have some of the exhibits tendered into evidence, I would recommend that they also prepare a file to be handed over to the Bench so that the Bench has the documents when they are needed. So much for the exhibits. I'd like to move on to the next topic, i.e., videos. I have a number of unanswered questions here. I have viewed all of the videos. This takes -- this would take several hours. What is the Prosecution going to do? Will it present the videos in the presence of a witness? I think the first witness who will call to testify is -- will testify on Stolac. The number of videos that show Stolac, do you intend viewing the video in the presence of the witness so that the witness says: Yes, that is my house, that is a village in which I lived, or do you intend, like it was the Hadzihasanovic/Kubura case, have a hearing dedicated to video viewing? I don't know whether you plan to do this, but I would like you to shed some light on your intentions. Mr. Mundis or Mr. Scott, can you please tell us how you intend to proceed with these videos.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sure there will be some video material that will be used with a particular witness. The example you just gave, a situation where a witness comes and there's very directly relevant video material for that witness, it maybe even shows the witness himself or herself or their home or something. So, yes, in some situations we might -- we would anticipate playing the video with the witness. Having said that, I fully expect that there will be other video material that at the end of the day will simply be presented to the Chamber as among our evidence, that might not be employed with any particular witness, will still be in the evidentiary record and we may play them at some time or they may simply be in the record and at some point when someone wants to look at them or consider them, they can be played.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, I have understood you well. You have said that some of the videos will be viewed in the presence of the witness and other videos or video material will be tendered into evidence. As far as I'm concerned - and I'm sure that my colleagues will hold the same view - the video material that has not been presented through a witness will have to be viewed by all and everyone and the comments will be in the transcript. And then we will decide whether the videos can be admitted into evidence or not because it so happens that some videos are 45-minute videos, some may last an hour or two hours, so this does pose a serious problem. So it is out of the question. We can't say to someone: I'm going to show you an excerpt of the video. Do you recognise the video? And then the video is admitted into evidence. When Judges deliberate, we look at the videos all over again and then we may pick up one or another item on the videos. So we have to see the video from beginning to end and I strongly recommend that all the lawyers see these videos, if they have not had time to do so yet. They then can usefully cross-examine the witness. This is a very time-consuming exercise because there are tens of hours of viewing, ten at least, but this is something you need to do. Mr. Scott, would you like to add anything as far as video material is concerned?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, obviously, Your Honour, based on what you just said, we will be guided by the Court's direction and I based on that, I anticipate that, as I said, some video material will be played with a particular witness, and based on what Your Honour has just indicated, there will come -- I suppose there will come a point in trial in which we will have to play other video material that has not been offered through a particular witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, I also have a question to put to you, a question which was put to me by one of the Judges, and I would like to know what your position is. Article 73 -- Rule 73 bis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence states as follows. This relates to the pre-trial conference: "After having heard the Prosecutor, the Trial Chamber may fix a number of crime sites or incidents comprised in one or more of the charges in respect of which evidence may be presented by the Prosecutor which, having regard to all the relevant circumstances, including the crimes charged in the indictment, their classification and nature, the places where they are alleged to have been committed, their scale and the victims of the crimes, are reasonably representative of the crimes charged." So I would like the Prosecution to spell this out for me. How does it understand or interpret this paragraph? Can the Trial Chamber cut down on the number of places or facts or crime-based facts because a Trial Chamber may feel that some of these may be a good example of what actually happened? So let me give you an example. Let's take the case of Prozor municipality. A number of things happened in Prozor, and the Chamber feels that paragraph 48 of the indictment should be upheld concerning the fate of two victims, Polic and Odzic, two victims in the case, and the Trial Chamber would not mention the other victims because it would feel that these two crimes sufficiently illustrate what happened in the Prozor municipality. Could things be understood this way, or another way of addressing the matter is to do the following: The Chamber would set the number of locations and number of victims according to what is written in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, this takes us back to what you said earlier today about whether the Judges would intervene at the beginning of the trial and, essentially, shape the indictment and tell the Prosecution what its case is or, on the other hand, that you would, as we've discussed today, give the Prosecution a certain amount of time, which we hope - which we hope - will be a sufficient amount of time to present a reasonable case, and then it will be up to the Prosecution to use its time as it sees fit. I very seriously believe that it is the second option which is the appropriate one and which strikes the correct balance between trial efficiency and the primacy of the Prosecutor for having the responsibility of presenting the case.
