We still have a system in which it is primarily -- first of all and primarily the Prosecutor's obligation and responsibility under the Statute to present her case. We would -- we would be very opposed in general - there might be exceptions - but we would be very opposed to the Chamber picking and choosing what parts of the indictment they would like us to present our case. If you tell me, Your Honour, that you give us 450 hours, then we will allocate that 450 hours as best we can to cover the indictment in the way that we think is the most appropriate way to present our case. It is still our case to present. In terms of whether something would be determined to be representative, Your Honour, we would only be able to do that if the Defence would then agree and say: Yes, we agree that if the Chamber finds the situation with these two victims happened in this particular way, the Defence would agree the Prosecution does not have to lead any other evidence and that the other matters will be taken as also established. So if the Defence is prepared to agree on that basis, then perhaps we could make some progress.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very quickly I shall give the floor to Mr. Karnavas and Kovacic as far as this issue is concerned. It's an important issue and I would like to know what their opinion is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Well, I do agree with Mr. Scott that it is their case, and I certainly don't want them appealing later on where they're claiming that the Trial Bench abused its discretion, and I assume that's what Mr. Scott was alluding to at one point, although he didn't say that. I think the Prosecution should be entitled to put on its case. I think that the suggestion that the Trial Chamber is making, however, is a reasonable one and one that certainly we are willing to assist in the event we can meet halfway with the Prosecutor. So we don't -- at least, this particular Defence does not preclude the possibility of sitting down with the Prosecutor. If we go this route of the dossier, for instance, and if we can -- if we can both agree -- both sides agree, I think we can move much quicker with fewer witnesses with respect to crime base. There is one technical issue with respect to the e-court; how do these dossiers get presented in an e-court fashion? I just merely mention that because it comes to mind. But I think we can go either way but I would certainly -- I would prefer to allow the Prosecutor to put on its case the way they see fit because it is their case. It's my job to challenge that at every step, and I don't want them to think that somehow they were unable to put on their case and then later on try to overturn something on appeal because they feel that they were unable to present their evidence to meet their burden of proof, which is what they have to carry throughout this case. And certainly I don't want them to feel that somehow the Trial Chamber abused its discretion in their view in the way they curtail their ability to present their evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Just very briefly, Mr. Kovacic, I think Mr. Karnavas has summed up this concept pretty well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... just about what I wanted to say. But since we are at the end of the conference, I am afraid that I will not have a situation -- that I will not know the situation for my client regarding his statement under Rule 84 bis regarding a time he would be allowed to speak. It is very important for me because we have to decide --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'm going to address this straight away. Mr. Scott, when you are going to present your case, how much time would you actually need?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, to use the stopwatch analogy that someone else has mentioned today, I have to say that I have not put it to a stopwatch. I think it will take probably a full session -- what we consider a trial day, a full session. I might, ultimately, do better than that, but having said that, having not put a stopwatch to it, it's conceivable it might go over into a second day, because at the moment, Your Honour, I think it would be most helpful to the Chamber to have a fairly extensive overview of the case and a review of the evidence, which could be quite substantial. So I think it will be at least one session. Approximately one session, but it might go over into a second day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. If you need one day, Mr. Praljak will also have a day then. If you need a day and a half, Mr. Praljak will then have a day and a half also. So I think we should be able to do everything in one day. From what I understood, Mr. Praljak, when making his opening statement, would like to be assisted by someone. It seems that he has a number of documents he would like to present. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I was more concentrated on the first issue. The second one is a practical nature, to have a person to aid him by presentation on the screen who helped in preparation and is specialist for PowerPoint presentation so people follow him. But however, since you mention the time, that it should be equal to the Prosecution, if I may raise one argument, Your Honour. None of the six Defences will make any opening statement. Nobody. And none of the accused, except Praljak, decided so. So I -- I am kindly asking you to permit my client whatever time may be, but to give him a fixed time, and we submitted -- we asked for six hours, but whatever you decide it -- that it would not be tied to the time which the Prosecution will spend. Because then he cannot organise properly, so we would like to know whether it is six hours regardless of how much the Prosecutor will take, or it is four hours, whatever you decide, or five hours, but it is very difficult to present this idea without knowing exactly what the time will be. And again, I'm repeating myself, nobody else will speak on the Defence side. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to say that six hours is a tremendous amount of time. He may want to go into the detail of some of these issues, but if he focuses on what is essentially -- what he is essentially charged with, I don't think he will need six hours. I would like to understand why he needs six hours. During the pre-trial conference he will be able to tell us why he actually needs six hours. And if he could send us an outline of his presentation, this will enable us to see where things stand. I can't tell you whether it's going to be five hours or six hours or four hours. He will have at least the same time as the Prosecution. For the rest, I don't know. We will see how he -- this will depend on what he wants to say. We can proceed two ways: Either he will make a political statement which -- or he will talk about the facts and address these facts from a criminal procedure standpoint. So this may require more time. Well, you can see this with him and tell him that this will be discussed at the pre-trial conference. Before winding up, I would like to move into closed session. There's one last point I wish to address before adjourning today.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before adjourning, then, the last Status Conference - I'm turning to you - would anybody like to take the floor on any particular matter which has not been addressed? I'm turning to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. What about the Defence teams?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I just have one minor request or issue to raise. I noted that there was a change of plea recently with Mr. Rajic. There was some indication that he might be a witness. He's on a witness list. Recently and on television his lawyer apparently had indicated that he was -- that he might be available to be testifying. I know that he's being debriefed and I know that there's another related issue that is rather relevant. What we would like, with respect to -- what we would like to know is whether the Prosecution has given us everything with respect to Mr. Rajic, that is, not only his statements but anything else during these debriefing sessions. And also, on any other issues, related issues, with respect to other cases and other investigations that are either directly or indirectly related to this particular indictment - and I'm sure the Prosecution knows what I'm talking about - we would like to make sure that we have all of that information. And so if we can make an inquiry at this point whether, one, they intend to provide us that information; and two, when can we expect it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The Defence is asking the Prosecution the following: Have they received everything which they are entitled to and raises Mr. Rajic's case. And the Defence wonders whether, after having met with the person in question, did you disclose to the Defence any document? Did you disclose any document to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe Mr. Rajic is on the witness list. There's no secret about that. That's -- they've known that since January. In terms of whether there's been any particular disclosure at this time, I can't say, frankly, off the top of my head. Counsel can always send a letter or call me and we can make these inquiries. We don't have to do it in the courtroom. I will have to check to see what the current situation is. As you know, and as counsel apparently knows, the sentencing hearing was just the other day and it may be that we have been waiting for that process to be finalised, but we will check on the matter and report back to counsel. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again, just for a point of clarification, as I understand it, Mr. Rajic is -- is a major witness, in a sense, for the Prosecution related to the Blaskic case. An incident in that particular indictment is also found in this particular indictment. I would like to know whether we're going to be getting all the information related to any investigations that are ongoing concerning the Blaskic case and anyone else involved in that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I believe, out of an abundance of caution, because I don't know what it is Mr. Karnavas is talking about, I know certain things in the Blaskic case are under seal, can we go into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, can we move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We are in open session. This Status Conference has come to an end. All the parties will be present at the pre-trial conference to be held on Tuesday, the 25th of April, 2006. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: adjourned at 2.06 p.m.
